results.title: Google takes down a massive Android TV botnet, but infected devices remain dangerous
results.author: techkritiko@gmail.com (Jay Bonggolto) , Jay Bonggolto
results.content:
Google has taken down a huge Android malware operation that turned over 1.3 million Android TV boxes into weapons for cyber criminals.
The company revealed that the operation was performed by Videostrong Technology, a device maker that has been accused of intentionally putting a hidden backdoor on its products and selling access to criminal affiliates.
The malware, dubbed XCPE or x.cpe, was directly embedded in the firmware of Android TV boxes sold under different brands. Google’s Threat Intelligence Group said that Videostrong developed the backdoor as a business, not letting it slip through accidentally. Criminal partners could use infected devices to generate fake ad views, reroute internet traffic through unsuspecting homes, and install more malware.
A backdoor that gives criminals control of your TV box
Google is particularly concerned about XCPE because it runs with Android system-level privileges. It connects to remote command-and-control servers, enabling attackers to silently install applications, execute shell commands, take screenshots, and collect device information.
Google also found that the malware could collect account information, application lists, and system logs. Some operators even used the ability to remotely access the devices to capture keystrokes and establish reverse shells.
Just removing the malware application isn’t enough, though. The backdoor can restore itself from a protected firmware partition on every device reboot. It can also affect Google Play Protect by changing the security settings, making it much more difficult to detect and remove.
The most common way the infection spreads is through Android TV boxes, but researchers also saw XCPE on other Android-based devices such as karaoke machines, telehealth equipment, and digital signage systems.
Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android
Google cuts off Videostrong and its criminal partners
Google worked with Japan’s National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI to take the operation down. Its complaint targeted command servers operated by Videostrong, as well as the infrastructure behind more than a dozen other families of malware.
The company also banned Videostrong and future subsidiaries from making certified Android devices or supplying software to certified manufacturers.
The disruption could spread even further. Disabling the command infrastructure used by criminal affiliates will cut off access to at least 10 million more compromised devices infected through different distribution channels, Google figures.
Infected Android TV boxes might need replacing
There is a catch for consumers, however: the takedown does not automatically remove XCPE from impacted hardware. According to security researchers, users should identify potentially compromised devices, disconnect them, and consider replacement rather than relying on an ordinary app uninstall.
Google also tightened its firmware integrity checks and manufacturer vetting process after it found that Videostrong used obfuscation to load malicious code after a device initially booted up.
Jay Bonggolto always keeps a nose for news. He has been writing about consumer tech for as long as he can remember, and he has used a variety of Android phones since falling in love with Jelly Bean. Send him a direct message via X or LinkedIn.

results.summary:
Google has dismantled a massive malware operation involving Videostrong Technology that compromised over 1.3 million Android TV boxes by embedding a persistent backdoor directly into device firmware.

### Key Points
- Google identified the XCPE malware, which grants attackers system-level privileges to install apps, capture keystrokes, and reroute internet traffic.
- The malware was pre-installed by manufacturer Videostrong Technology on various Android-based devices, including TV boxes, karaoke machines, and digital signage.
- Because the malicious code resides in a protected firmware partition, it automatically reinstalls itself upon device reboot, rendering standard app removal ineffective.
- Google collaborated with international law enforcement and security firms to disable command-and-control servers, potentially impacting 10 million additional compromised devices.
- Google has banned Videostrong from producing certified Android devices and implemented stricter firmware integrity checks for all manufacturers.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights a significant supply chain vulnerability where hardware manufacturers intentionally embed malware at the firmware level. Consumers using affected devices may need to replace their hardware entirely, as the deep-seated nature of the infection makes standard security software unable to fully remediate the threat.

results.title: Black voters could sway the midterms in surprising places
results.author: Heather Digby Parton
results.content:
Loss aversion is a phenomenon in psychology and behavioral economics. Defined simply, it means that the pain experienced from a loss is felt twice as much as winning. In politics, that intensity manifests itself in motivation. If you take something away from people, they are going to feel it more acutely than promising them something, and the theft produces a backlash.
That’s what appears to be happening right now with Black voters. Across the country, they have been lining up to vote early, presumably against Donald Trump and the Republican Party’s MAGA agenda, in astonishing numbers, particularly in the South. That this comes only six months after the Supreme Court gutted the Voting Rights Act in Louisiana v. Callais should not come as a surprise.
In the Trump era, Republicans have become experienced at taking rights away from the American people. For women, it was the roll back of their constitutional rights when the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, sparking a backlash in that year’s midterm elections. Since Trump returned to office in January 2025, immigrants have come under assault from a xenophobic administration intent on carrying out mass deportations via masked, secret police rampaging through neighborhoods. The LGBTQ+ community, and trans people in particular, have seen their rights stripped away.
To many Black Americans, the GOP’s agenda and behavior will not have come as a surprise. After all, it’s been at the core of their history going back to before the country’s founding.
These policies have come as a shock to some Americans who never thought Trump would go there, and they have also opened the eyes of others to the cruelty at the heart of MAGA, overseen by the highest court of the land. But to many Black Americans, the GOP’s agenda and behavior will not have come as a surprise. After all, it’s been at the core of their history going back to before the country’s founding.
Black Americans know what it means to have their civil rights taken away from them. They understand fully the fear of being targeted by brutal, marauding gangs of armed men. In the decade following the Civil War and the passage of the 14th and 15th Amendments, Black people began to participate fully in civil society. Mississippi elected two Black U.S. senators and a lieutenant governor, and former slaves and their offspring enjoyed freedom of speech, movement and opportunity. But the white members of Southern society would not let that stand, and as soon as the federal government withdrew its troops, they stepped in with legal and social barriers to deny Black Americans their rights, this time backed by vigilante and state violence that became Jim and Jane Crow.
Almost a century had passed by the time Lyndon Johnson signed the Civil Rights Act in 1964 and the Voting Rights Act in 1965, a period characterized by subjugation and violence by the white majority. But Black America kept fighting, against all odds, until they won.
This year, we have seen yet another attempt by reactionary politicians and judges to turn back the clock. After the Callais decision, several Southern states reverted immediately to form and radically redrew their congressional districts to favor the white majority, making it much more difficult for voters to elect a Black federal and state representatives.
They may come to regret that decision. This isn’t 1955 (or 1855) anymore, as much as Donald Trump would like to make it so, and the Black community is once again mobilizing. According to experts, early voting data is showing something unexpected: The vote is being driven by young voters rather than just those who went through the earlier battles. It’s muscle memory for the Black community.
After 2024, when Trump won a surprising 15% of the Black vote — nearly doubling his share of 8% in the 2020 election — Republicans thought they were defying history to make great inroads within the community. Then, incredibly, the administration began attacking Black America. The result is what some politicos are calling a “Blacklash,” and it could very well be decisive in some places where nobody expected the Democrats to do well. And even if it doesn’t result in flipping seats, it’s a shot across the bow.
Want more sharp takes on politics? Sign up for our free newsletter, Standing Room Only, written by Amanda Marcotte, now also a weekly show on YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.
In Mississippi, prosecutor and former judge Scott Colom, who is Black, is running an excellent race against Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, the GOP incumbent. Colom has made some very clever advertisements which have garnered a lot of national attention, but Republicans and Democrats alike had largely ignored the race until just a couple of months ago. Polling has tightened, and the GOP has dispatched an influx of luminaries, including Trump himself. For the first time in years, Democrats from Bill Clinton to Kamala Harris, along with a long line of senators, have descended on the state to support Colom. Former President Barack Obama even cut an ad for him. Mississippi has the largest population of Black voters of any state in the country. If Colum gets a big Black turnout with just enough disaffected whites, he could win.
Louisiana, after giving birth to the case that saw the Supreme Court’s conservative majority gut the Voting Rights Act, has been winnowed down to one majority Black district in a state that is one-third African-American. But there has been a surge in Black participation akin to what is seen in presidential years, which could prove decisive in a race for Louisiana’s open Senate seat that has been a sleeper until the last couple of weeks. According to a recent poll, Republican Julia Letlow and Democrat Jamie Davis are tied. Among voters who have already cast their ballot, Davis — who is Black — holds a six-point advantage, and 34% of early votes have been cast by Black Louisianans.
Then there’s South Carolina, which has seen Trump make three desperate appearances to shore up Darline Graham’s torpid campaign. The endangered incumbent, foisted upon South Carolina Republicans by the president himself following the sudden death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, is not getting the job done. As numbers cruncher Nate Silver pointed out, a recent New York Times poll showing the race essentially tied is not an outlier; she is in deep trouble. As of late October, the Times reports, “Black voters accounted for around 28 percent of early votes, while making up around 20 percent of the overall electorate in recent cycles. The trend is not unlike what we’re seeing in Georgia and North Carolina thus far.” If that holds true through Election Day, we could see the biggest upset of the whole campaign, largely due to Black South Carolinians saying “Enough is enough.”
In a few short hours, all the ads, mailers, signs and rallies will mercifully come to an end. I am cautiously optimistic, but like many, I’ll never celebrate prematurely again. There is good reason, though, to feel more positive than we have in a long time. Trump and his acolytes have overreached. Opting for the big tech credo of “move fast and break things,” they vastly overestimated their abilities — and the American people’s tolerance.
They have also aroused a group of Americans who know what it is to lose their rights and privileges. With all that history and so many battles, Black Americans have shown what it takes to never give up.
Read more
about the 2026 midterms
results.summary:
Black voters are mobilizing in record numbers across the American South, driving a significant surge in early voting turnout in response to recent GOP policies and judicial decisions.

### Key Points
- Early voting data shows Black participation rates exceeding recent election cycles in states like South Carolina, Georgia, and North Carolina.
- The surge follows the Supreme Court’s decision in *Louisiana v. Callais*, which allowed states to redraw congressional districts in ways that favor white majorities.
- Competitive Senate races in Mississippi and Louisiana have tightened significantly as Democratic candidates benefit from increased Black voter engagement.
- Analysts attribute the trend to "loss aversion," where voters are more motivated to protect existing rights than to pursue new political promises.
- Younger Black voters are playing a central role in this mobilization, signaling a shift in traditional voter demographics.

### Why it Matters
This surge in voter participation suggests that aggressive policy shifts and the erosion of voting protections may be triggering a powerful electoral backlash. If these turnout trends hold through Election Day, they could fundamentally alter the outcomes of key congressional races and challenge Republican efforts to expand their influence within the Black electorate.

results.title: North Korea rejects U.S. allegation over $6 billion Binance crypto heist
results.author: By Jack Kim, Kyu-seok Shim and Rae Wee
results.content:
By Jack Kim, Kyu-seok Shim and Rae Wee
SEOUL/SINGAPORE, Nov 3 (Reuters) - Asset outflows from Binance have normalised and the company was in "very strong financial health", its co-CEO said, as North Korea dismissed as "absurd rhetoric" US allegations that it was behind a $6.3 billion cryptocurrency heist on its platform.
The world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, whose customers had withdrawn a net $4.72 billion as of Monday after it was hit with what could be the largest-ever financial heist last week, has also launched a campaign to stem outflows and woo new users.
"In the first 24 hours, there was a spike in terms of withdrawals, as can be expected. But after that ... it's pretty much normalised," Richard Teng told a Hong Kong Fintech Week event on Tuesday.
"The company is in very strong financial health," he said, adding 95% of the affected tokens had been replenished. "This is something that we can cover. We are able to do so."
The crypto exchange was seeing "hourly deposits exceed withdrawals", Binance said in an X post earlier on Tuesday, adding that it reflected improving user activity and stabilising flows.
The FBI said at the weekend that North Korea was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion in crypto assets, a crime that sent shockwaves through the industry.
Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, said the US allegations proved Washington remained hostile towards Pyongyang, according to a report on Tuesday by state news agency KCNA.
Pyongyang has not responded to US President Donald Trump's overtures, made earlier this year, to resume summit diplomacy. In the wake of the US allegations, Kim Yo Jong said North Korea had "issues to reconsider" over what she called US hostility.
"The FBI is trying to brand the DPRK as a 'cyber criminal state,' claiming that it obtained information that a hacking organization 'supported' by the DPRK was involved in the incident," KCNA quoted Kim Yo Jong as saying.
"But the US assertion is absurd rhetoric and nothing new," said Kim, a ruling party official. DPRK is short for the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.
"It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds."
REVENUE STREAM
North Korea faces growing scrutiny over cryptocurrency theft, which analysts say is a key source of funds for its weapons programmes.
Cybersecurity experts say North Korean hackers are among the world's most prolific crypto thieves and the proceeds help fund the country's efforts to develop nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles capable of hitting the United States.
North Korea has stolen cryptocurrency worth $7.6 billion this year, more than in any previous year, according to estimates by blockchain analytics firm Elliptic.
North Korea denies allegations linking it to cryptocurrency theft and other cybercrimes.
Analysts in Seoul said Pyongyang's unusually swift response likely reflected concern that the allegation could lead to tighter efforts to disrupt revenue streams that North Korea is accused of using to finance its weapons.
"With sanctions already in place, cryptocurrency theft has become one of North Korea's key channels for securing funds for regime maintenance and weapons development," said Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University's Institute for Far Eastern Studies.
Additional US measures targeting crypto wallets, laundering networks and cryptocurrency exchanges could choke off an important source of revenue, Lim said.
South Korea's central bank estimated North Korea's gross domestic product at 47.18 trillion won ($35.09 billion) in 2025, meaning the Binance theft could be equivalent to about a sixth of its economic output.
Blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis estimated 89% of crypto hack losses in 2026 were linked to North Korea, up from 15% in 2021. It said the average reported loss per hack rose from $50.65 million in 2021 to $185.65 million in 2026.
"I guess you could call it big game hunting, where they're targeting these larger exchanges that may take more time and more complexity to be able to do ... but the payoff can be relatively large," said Alec Zebrick, senior manager of Asia-Pacific Global Services at Chainalysis.
North Korea is one of the world's most impoverished countries but has poured resources secured through illicit means and activities banned under UN Security Council resolutions into its missile and nuclear programmes.
Kim Yo Jong said North Korea would "reconsider" unspecified issues in light of the "very unpleasant US hostile attitude", without elaborating. North Korea has not publicly responded to Trump's offers to resume summit diplomacy.
BINANCE WITHDRAWALS
Binance launched a campaign on Monday offering fee rebates, rewards to eligible users who rack up at least $10,000 in cumulative trading volume, as well as annual percentage rates of up to 10% on certain yield-generating products.
The exchange's "community appreciation campaign" will run through November 21, a post on its website showed.
Binance, which froze withdrawals for more than two days after the hack and then started allowing customers to withdraw again on Sunday morning in some assets, reopened withdrawals for more assets on Tuesday.
Since the resumption of withdrawals, Binance has seen net outflows amounting to around 3% of the assets on its platform, it said on Monday, a relatively modest figure that analysts said suggested customer confidence had largely held up.
"The relatively contained price reaction suggests a degree of maturity and resilience," said Maksym Repa, head of DeFi at Lombard, a Bitcoin finance protocol backed by Franklin Templeton.
"Investors appear to be distinguishing between a security failure at a centralised exchange and a problem with the Bitcoin network itself."
($1 = 1,344.4300 won)
(Reporting by Jack Kim, Kyu-seok Shim and Maggie Grether in Seoul; Rae Wee and Ankur Banerjee in Singapore; and Summer Zhen in Hong Kong; Editing by Ed Davies, Sumeet Chatterjee, Stephen Coates and Saad Sayeed)
results.summary:
Binance co-CEO Richard Teng reports that asset outflows have normalized following a $6.3 billion heist, while North Korea dismisses U.S. allegations of involvement in the massive cyberattack.

### Key Points
- Binance experienced $4.72 billion in net outflows following a major security breach, but the exchange claims 95% of affected tokens have been replenished.
- The FBI alleges North Korea is responsible for the $6.3 billion theft, a claim Pyongyang official Kim Yo Jong labeled as "absurd rhetoric."
- Blockchain analytics firm Elliptic estimates North Korea has stolen $7.6 billion in cryptocurrency this year to fund its nuclear and ballistic missile programs.
- Binance has launched a "community appreciation campaign" offering fee rebates and yield incentives to stabilize its user base through November 21.
- Chainalysis reports that North Korea was linked to 89% of all crypto hack losses in 2026, up significantly from 15% in 2021.

### Why it Matters
The incident highlights the growing vulnerability of centralized cryptocurrency exchanges to state-sponsored cyberattacks aimed at bypassing international sanctions. If the U.S. implements stricter regulations on crypto wallets and exchanges, it could significantly disrupt a primary revenue stream used to finance North Korea's weapons development.

results.title: Midterm elections 2026: all the news
results.author: Lauren Feiner
results.content:
The 2026 midterm elections will determine the scope of President Donald Trump’s power in his final two years in office, and signal what voters care about going into the 2028 presidential election. While this year’s races are expected to be most broadly defined by affordability issues, there are several topics impacting the tech industry that appear to be on voters’ minds.
Among them are concerns about data centers, and whether voters will have to bear the burden of higher energy costs, AI safety, and the rapid expansion of surveillance technology through Flock. There’s also the question of how to tax billionaires’ wealth in California, a topic that has driven heavy tech spending and creative stock class structures meant to keep tech executives from fleeing the state should a ballot measure pass.
The next Congress is likely to continue grappling with how to regulate AI, and stem the data center backlash, among other issues. How that conversation shapes up, and which tech CEOs are hauled to testify on Capitol Hill, will be shaped by the outcome of November 3rd.
- Data center developers are poised to face a more restrictive building environment after voters across the country voted in candidates who favor moratoriums and ballot measures that put more obstacles on their expansion, delivering a stinging blow to a central pillar of the AI industry. Of voters polled by NBC News on Election Day, 76 percent said they opposed data centers in their communities. Dozens of local communities voted directly to restrict development through ballot measures. And upset winners like Texas Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa and Michigan’s Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed support moratoriums on development. Read Article >
- Maine Republican Susan Collins concedes Senate seat in a tech-fueled race. The longtime senator counted tech executives like Palantir CEO Alex Karp and venture capitalists Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz among her donors. Democratic challenger Troy Jackson also received some billionaire support, but no obvious tech ties. Maine almost became the first state to pause data centers, before the governor vetoed the moratorium.
- Democrat projected to win Ohio seat that Republicans warned could spell trouble for data centers. NBC News projects Democrat Sherrod Brown will win back his former Senate seat from Republican Jon Husted, who Brown had labeled “the face of data centers.” The National Republican Senatorial Committee warned in a leaked August memo that if Husted loses “and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice — and they will not go near the next one.”
- Data center-dense Texas turns blue. Both Democrats James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa are projected by NBC News to win their Senate and gubernatorial races, respectively. Hinojosa has called for a moratorium on data center development in the state, while Talarico has favored ending tax incentives and creating an “AI dividend” for Americans to share in profits.
- Data center backlash wasn’t quite enough to flip Florida. The pro-data center Republican Byron Donalds has won the race for governor, according to the AP. He beat Democrat David Jolly with just over 50 percent of the vote — a far tighter margin than predecessor Ron DeSantis in 2022.
- Democrats leaned into Big Tech and AI opposition this cycle. Democratic candidates touted their credentials taking on the tech industry far more than in prior election cycles, an analysis by public policy group Reset Tech finds. Between 2020 and 2024, only two Democratic ads used the phrase “Big Tech.” From 2025 to 2026, that number was 154.
- Fulton County, GA may need to rescan 1,000 ballots tonight because of scanner malfunctions. A county election official asked the election board for approval to rescan ballots from two scanners experiencing equipment issues. One scanner seemed to wrongly display that it had a paper jam, CBS News reports, while another displayed an error after a voter accidentally rolled over its cable with a wheelchair.
- Things still seem to be going fairly smoothly. The nonpartisan Election Protection Coalition says it’s received over 8,000 hotline calls today, but the reported concerns are fairly standard for large elections. Rev. Dr. Katie Sexton Wood, executive director of the Arizona Faith Network, says there’s been no verified reports of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) near Arizona polling spots.
- Michigan officials contacted DOJ about reports of election monitors speaking with poll workers. State officials got reports that DOJ monitors asked poll workers in Dearborn for their training materials, Michigan Attorney General office spokesperson Danny Wimmer confirms. The DOJ’s team overseeing Michigan monitors told state officials such actions were not part of their training, Wimmer says, and that the team would follow up. But in a statement to The Verge, DOJ spokesperson Kiersten Pels says the questions monitors asked were “typical questions about election official training” that are standard on forms provided to monitors and the same as those asked under the previous administration. Pels added that the DOJ has not confimed that monitors have asked for training materials, but told Michigan officials they’d remind monitors they can ask about training, but “don’t need to request training materials.” Update: Added DOJ statement.
- It’s the midterms! Here’s a fun fact for you as you head to the polls: Gas prices today are the highest ever recorded for a US Election Day. The national average for a gallon of gasoline is $4.12 and $6.28 for a gallon of diesel, according to GasBuddy. Meanwhile, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which is maintained by the US Department of Energy as a safeguard during energy crises, is down to 282.2 million barrels of crude, the lowest level in 44 years. Read Article >
- Severe weather is affecting some voters across the country. In Florida, more than 20 polling sites are being moved due to intense flooding. Storms in the Southwest have also impacted some polling locations in Colorado, Newsweek reports, while Utah will let some voters impacted by flooding return ballots electronically, and Arizona officials are warning voters to check travel updates.
- A ballot scanner issue is impacting a New York suburb. Polling sites across Westchester County are experiencing an issue with their voting machines, but officials say residents can still safely cast their ballots. Election officials have a backup protocol in place to ensure voting can continue.
- Election protection hotline has received 3,000 calls this morning. The nonpartisan coalition running the 866-OUR-VOTE hotline says the calls range from asking about general information, to reporting long lines, lack of signage, or voting equipment issues. Texas, Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and New York account for the most calls. So far, no calls about federal agents at the polls.
- DOJ sends 1,000 election monitors to watch polls in every state. Federal election monitors are a standard procedure, but this year the Trump administration has expanded it to the “largest monitoring effort in history.” States have prepared to make sure they don’t interfere, as the administration has taken several steps this year to assert more oversight of state-run elections.
- A high-stakes California ballot measure pitched as a fast track for “essential” infrastructure could wind up giving data center developers a loophole to evade public scrutiny, environmental advocates warn. Proposition 45 would shorten timelines for state-mandated environmental assessments for eligible projects and make it more difficult for residents to challenge those projects in court. Proponents say passing the measure would help alleviate the state’s housing shortage and meet rising electricity demand with new renewable energy projects. Environmental groups and some legal experts, however, warn that data center developers backing the proposition could escape scrutiny if Prop 45 becomes law. Read Article >
- Another election year, another tech company war room. OpenAI is the latest tech company (and according to Politico, the first major AI company) to set up a command center for fighting election misinfo and abuse of its systems, approaching the second major AI-era US election: The Election Operations Center will begin running this week until all votes are counted, to identify the potential spread of misinformation or other efforts to disrupt the elections. It’s meant in large part to combat abuse of the company’s own tools like ChatGPT, monitoring real-time events and fielding reports of unexpected behavior from models or cases of suspected violations of their platform’s terms.
- Ask Texas NAACP president Gary Bledsoe what it’s been like to see data center developers descend upon Austin and its surrounding suburbs and he can rattle off project after project facing opposition from locals. There’s the fight in Taylor over plans to build a data center at a site that’s supposed to be a park. Temple, around 40 miles away, is another sore spot, Bledsoe says. The mayor and City Council members there face recall attempts over data center developments. And some 30 miles outside of Austin, San Marcos became the first city in all of Texas to ban data centers. Read Article >
- If there’s one issue that seems to activate all kinds of voters in 2026, it’s data centers. The rapid buildout of these massive server storage facilities — and the infrastructure construction and expenses that come with them — has sparked local opposition in communities across the country and become a major issue in many congressional and gubernatorial campaigns. At the same time, tech money has been pouring into many of these races. Leading the Future, a super PAC backed by venture capitalist Marc Andreessen and OpenAI President Greg Brockman, has already spent $45 million in a year. And Public First Action, an Anthropic-backed group that says it supports AI safeguards, says it’s raised $80 million. Both have funded Democratic and Republican-aligned groups. Other super PACs see an opportunity to push for stricter AI policies, like the recently created Tomorrow Together, which launched $4 million in ads for battleground House races, with messages about data center development and AI safety. Read Article >
- Two years ago, University of Houston student Vasant Bhatt was doing everything he could to help Republicans regain power. He knocked doors for Sen. Ted Cruz’s reelection campaign and helped organize his community for Donald Trump, two victories he, like many other Republicans, celebrated in 2024. But this week, Bhatt did something unexpected: He voted for Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, and he publicly urged others to do the same. Bhatt, whose father is a small-business owner, tells The Verge he was initially drawn to the Republican Party due to its economic principles. “The strong belief in individual liberty and limited government,” he says, led him to identify as a conservative. More recently, however, another aspect of his family’s experience has driven him away from the party. As an Indian American, Bhatt feels increasingly unwelcome in a party where racist rhetoric is becoming far too common. Read Article >
- Meta made a deal to keep Mark Zuckerberg from leaving California over its billionaire tax. It said in a filing that Zuckerberg “was evaluating relocating his primary residence” if California’s Proposition 40 passes. As Bloomberg reports, Meta’s board issued special shares so that he wouldn’t have to leave: Zuckerberg gets non-voting shares he can sell for liquidity without reducing his voting control. In return, he has committed to remain in California — or wherever Meta is headquartered — for eight years while he remains in a full-time leadership role.
- Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance said on Tuesday that the Trump administration was giving right-wing YouTuber Nick Shirley $10,000 and launching a $25 million bounty program for members of the public to report fraud. In December 2025, Shirley published a viral video alleging fraud at daycares in Minnesota that were operated by members of the local Somali community. Shirley lingered in parking lots and asked to enter childcare centers, taking refusals as evidence that the centers weren’t actually caring for children. The video quickly went viral, triggering a massive governmental response: Federal immigration agents descended on the Minneapolis area, and the Trump administration froze Minnesota’s federal funding for childcare. Shirley has since visited other states in the US under similar pretenses, showing up unannounced to grocery stores and hospice centers in search of evidence of fraud. Vance and others in the administration publicly praised Shirley, who has since become a mainstay in the MAGA-aligned content creator ecosystem. He’s helped popularize a genre of so-called independent journalism popular on the right in which content creators and influencers confront businesses or people they suspect of fraud or crime as the basis for their online content. Harassment — or even immigration crackdowns — often follow. Read Article >
- Democrats could win back control of Congress this November, and if they do, they’ll need to decide how to approach one of the country’s newest and thorniest political issues: AI. Polls predict Democrats will flip at least one chamber of Congress in the midterm elections, which would put committee leadership back in their hands. That could usher in a wave of newfound scrutiny for AI companies. Top Democrats on key committees have already signaled their willingness to press the industry on tax credits tied to data centers and recent hacking incidents, and would be able to set committee agendas if they take over, allowing them to call CEOs to testify in Congress and demand documents that explain companies’ inner workings. Read Article >
- Tech billionaires have reportedly donated over $340 million to fight a wealth tax in California. According to The Guardian, the campaign they’re funding is spending over $1 million per day trying to defeat Proposition 40, which would enact a one-time 5 percent tax on California’s billionaires. Google co-founder Sergey Brin is reportedly the biggest donor, contributing at least $102 million, alongside other tech executives: The donors to the no campaign are a who’s who of Silicon Valley, including the Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, DoorDash CEO Tony Xu, Stripe CEO Patrick Collison, crypto magnate Chris Larsen and several prominent venture capitalists.
- Elon Musk has handed out at least $276 million to Republican groups since July, The New York Times reports, making him both the party’s top known donor and the biggest established midterm donor. $158 million of that money — one of the largest political donations in American history — has been funneled into the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC that aims to secure and maintain a Republican Senate majority. Among others, it’s fighting to retain the party’s Senate seat in Texas, which serves as a major hub for Musk’s business empire. He’s also donated over $76 million to America PAC, a super PAC Musk founded in 2024 that canvasses for hard-to-reach Republican voters. Smaller amounts have also been given to other conservative groups, including: Read Article >
- One messy database is threatening to disenfranchise thousands or even millions of registered voters, while leaving even more at risk of intimidation or data breaches, in the name of solving a problem that barely exists. As the 2026 midterm elections approach, election and privacy experts are sounding alarms about the Department of Homeland Security’s Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) Program, which President Donald Trump’s administration has expanded to ostensibly catch noncitizens voting. Experts say that amounts to a dangerous, error-prone effort to centralize voter data. “The federal government doesn’t have the authority to do any of that and doesn’t have the expertise either,” says Eileen O’Connor, senior counsel at the Brennan Center. “Inserting themselves into the day-to-day functioning of state elections is unprecedented and disturbing.” Read Article >

results.title: Is Your Echo Show Display Filling With AI Slop? I Found How to Turn It Off
results.author: Tyler Lacoma
results.content:
With Amazon announcing a new Echo Show 16 to square off with Apple’s upcoming HomeView, the smart displays are having a moment, but I’ve noticed something seems off. In the past week or two, my Echo Show has started showing me a lot of lazy, annoying AI-generated ads under a playback feature called Created For You. So I figured out how to improve my experience with a few settings changes.
Not only is this AI slop vague and accompanied by poorly generated images, but it also doesn’t seem to have anything to do with my recorded interests or personalization, either. The slides range from questions about squirrels finding nuts and how to make cornfield mazes to facts about daylight saving time. Basically, it’s very general content I don’t really care about and don’t want showing on a central display at home.
I suspect Amazon is pushing its AI podcasts and similar chatty content with this latest round of generated ads, but if you’re not interested in viewing any of these canned clips, they can come across as irksome. So I reviewed my settings options and found out how to push my Show display away from these creations and toward more interesting content.
More from CNET
How do I turn off these AI-generated slides?
The good news is you can control what your Echo Show, well, shows you — but you have to know what settings to change. This isn’t very easy through the Alexa app, but I found a better way using the Show’s own touchscreen controls. Here’s what to do when you have a minute.
First, when an AI slide like this appears, tap the three-dot menu button and tap the thumbs-down option to indicate your dislike. It’s not a perfect solution, but it should help start weeding out these types of ads.
Next, swipe down on your Echo Show device to access the main menu, and choose Settings. Then choose Display & Appearance, and head to Content Categories.
Here you have two options. You can manually turn off all the categories you don’t want to see, especially those connected to the AI slop that you’ve been seeing. Keep focus on topics that you’re interested in if you still want to see other related content. You can also toggle the Rotate Once setting on, which will show you Amazon’s slides only once, my preferred option for handling this kind of unwanted content.
As an alternative, you can switch your Echo Show to show only a photo album of your choosing. I like getting some Alexa recommendations like recipes and updates, so this option isn’t for me, but if you have a good photo album to share with Alexa, you can limit your slides to only your own content.
With these settings adjusted, you should see far fewer AI-generated images and more slides tailored to your own interests. I’ll keep an eye on my Echo Shows and let you know if anything changes, but this has worked well for me so far.
results.summary:
Amazon is introducing the new Echo Show 16 while users report frustration over intrusive, AI-generated advertisements appearing on their existing smart display devices across the Echo lineup.

### Key Points
- Amazon recently announced the Echo Show 16 to compete with Apple’s upcoming HomeView smart display.
- Users report that the "Created For You" feature is displaying irrelevant, AI-generated content and images on Echo Show devices.
- Owners can provide feedback by tapping the three-dot menu on a slide and selecting the thumbs-down icon.
- Content categories can be managed by navigating to Settings, then Display & Appearance, and finally Content Categories on the device.
- Users can limit unwanted slides by enabling the "Rotate Once" setting or by configuring the display to show only personal photo albums.

### Why it Matters
The rise of AI-generated content on smart home devices highlights a growing tension between platform monetization and user experience. As companies integrate generative tools into hardware, providing clear opt-out mechanisms is essential to maintaining consumer trust and device utility.

results.title: Japanese Arcade Machines Have Been Taken Down By A Major Hack Of Sega’s Services
results.author: Alicia Haddick
results.content:
The online services of a number of Japanese arcade games, including heavy hitters such as Bandai Namco’s Taiko no Tatsujin and Sega’s Initial D: The Arcade, have been forced offline due to a widespread hack of online services ALL.net and Aime. As of November 1st at 3 p.m. local time in Japan, all services involving these networks have been affected, while Sega Fave—the Sega subsidiary in charge of the service—investigates the breach.
The ALL.net service is an online network that allows machines in Japanese arcades to connect to the internet, providing online matches, online leaderboards, sharing save data and other similar services. Meanwhile, Aime is a service working with NFC cards that stores player information, tapped at any machine for use. The account number on these cards can then be accessed online by Sega to verify this information. Though this is a service provided by Sega, the tool is also licensed by companies like Bandai Namco for Idolm@ster TOURS and Taiko no Tatsujin, and by Sega itself for non-arcade services such as their Lucky Kuji Online random prize service.
According to Sega, a third party gained unauthorized access to these services, and the company is now investigating to learn the extent of the situation. In the meantime, the services are down, but Sega is already confirming that no customer or business partner data has been breached, and that payment information was not stored on the affected servers.
For many of the most popular games in Japanese arcades, especially rhythm games, this service is vital to their operation. This is obviously seriously affecting arcades which cannot operate these machines. Two days later, the service has yet to return, with many social media users sharing images of arcades with many of their usually bustling machines blocked from public use. Others are limiting games to offline use only to allow some games to remain playable during the outage. Sega updated its notice November 2 to say the investigation is expected to take some time to complete.
 早く治ってー pic.twitter.com/7ZVVfF5WzI
— はるぼー (@harutaiko2405) November 2, 2026
The nature of the unauthorized access has yet to be disclosed, and the incident follows Sega taking down the same service for multiple days at the end of last month in order to address the PHP exploit. In response to this, the company also chose to reopen the service by limiting access to Aime and ALL.net services only to Japan, resulting in complaints from the growing contingent of international fans of these arcade games. Now, the games are offline once again, with no clear date as to when they will resume service.
results.summary:
Sega Fave has suspended its ALL.net and Aime online services following a security breach, forcing popular Japanese arcade games like Taiko no Tatsujin offline since November 1.

### Key Points
- Sega Fave confirmed unauthorized third-party access to the ALL.net network and Aime NFC card system.
- Affected titles include major arcade games such as Bandai Namco’s Taiko no Tatsujin and Sega’s Initial D: The Arcade.
- Sega reports that no customer payment information or personal data was compromised during the security incident.
- Arcades across Japan are currently operating machines in limited offline modes or blocking access entirely while the investigation continues.
- This breach follows a previous service outage in late October intended to address a specific PHP exploit.

### Why it Matters
The outage disrupts the core functionality of Japan’s competitive arcade scene, which relies on these networks for leaderboards, save data, and online matchmaking. While no data was stolen, the prolonged downtime highlights the vulnerability of centralized gaming infrastructure and the significant operational impact on physical arcade businesses.

results.title: Here's Why You Shouldn't Use AI to Vote
results.author: David Gilbert
results.content:
As Americans go to the polls today, many will have had their decision about who to vote for informed by an artificial intelligence–powered chatbot.
Around 50 percent of recently surveyed US adults have at one time used an AI chatbot, and 8 percent say they have used these tools ahead of the midterms to find information on candidates and policies, according to Pew Research.
But a lot of information from these chatbots is out of date and has been hallucinated or sourced from partisan websites.
Even supposedly nonpartisan chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, and Google’s Gemini have been found wanting when it comes to questions about the midterms.
Just last week, Google’s AI Mode refused to provide the results of the 2020 elections, and the company’s Gemini chatbot said the deadline to request a mail-in ballot in Pennsylvania was November 3, rather than the real deadline of October 27, according to research by Forum AI.
According to the Forum AI research, almost 40 percent of election answers given by all the mainstream chatbots contained at least one factual error. In August, when Forum AI’s researchers asked why someone should vote for North Carolina congressman Don Davis, Claude gave a response that conflated the lawmaker with a “former school superintendent” of the same name.
Google and Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment. Open AI directed WIRED to a blog outlining the company’s approach to elections in 2026.
Part of the problem is that chatbots are reliant on an increasingly problematic pool of online information. Research by NewsGuard found that mainstream chatbots cite so-called “pink slime” websites nearly 50 percent of the time when asked about candidates and policies related to the midterms. Pink slime sites present as mainstream news websites but are in fact funded by political or ideological groups and individuals.
Ahead of the midterms, many more of these sites have sprung up, and chatbots are paying attention. The worst offender, according to NewsGuard, was OpenAI’s ChatGPT, which cited the pink slime sites in more than 70 percent of searches, while xAI’s Grok chatbot performed best, citing pink slime sites in 30 percent of cases.
“I don't think that most Americans are prepared to navigate an election in the age of consumer AI,” Nina Jankowicz, executive director of the American Sunlight Project and a former disinformation czar during the Biden administration, tells WIRED. “One of the problems is that executives and companies have really overpromised on what AI is capable of. It has to ingest this information from somewhere, and often those sources are not very good. And it's predictive, so if it doesn't know the answer, it does frequently make things up.”
results.summary:
Mainstream artificial intelligence chatbots are providing inaccurate information to voters, with research showing nearly 40 percent of election-related responses contain factual errors or rely on unreliable partisan sources.

### Key Points
- Pew Research indicates 8 percent of U.S. adults have used AI chatbots to research candidates and policies ahead of the current election cycle.
- Forum AI found that Google’s Gemini and other mainstream tools frequently hallucinate data, including incorrect mail-in ballot deadlines and conflated candidate biographies.
- NewsGuard reports that chatbots often cite "pink slime" websites—partisan outlets disguised as news—in up to 70 percent of election-related queries.
- OpenAI’s ChatGPT cited these unreliable sources in 70 percent of searches, while xAI’s Grok performed best with a 30 percent citation rate.
- Major AI companies, including Google and Anthropic, have faced criticism for failing to provide accurate, nonpartisan information regarding election logistics and candidate records.

### Why it Matters
The reliance on AI for political research poses a significant risk to voter accuracy as chatbots frequently prioritize biased or fabricated content over verified news. This trend highlights a growing gap between the public's trust in AI tools and the technology's current inability to reliably navigate complex, high-stakes political information.

results.title: Millions of Android TV boxes came with malware, and Google's certification missed it
results.author: Hamed Paydarfar
results.content:
Summary
- XCPE backdoor preinstalled on 1.3M set-top boxes by Videostrong, creating a botnet for fraud, theft and traffic routing
- Videostrong passed Google's certification by hiding malware that activated only after the first boot.
- Google says it has now cut ties with Videostrong and tightened reviews.
Google and its partners recently shared the news of a now-dismantled backdoor that was preinstalled on more than 1.3 million set-top boxes, turning them into nodes in a botnet. According to the company's official report, the XCPE malware was deliberately deployed by Videostrong, which is an Android device manufacturer.
The backdoor was built directly into the firmware of the affected models over several years. Infected boxes were used for things like ad fraud and data theft. Moreover, units had the ability to route other people's traffic through the owner's internet connection, which put anyone using the same network as an infected Android TV box at risk.
These boxes passed Google's certification for years
And it makes you wonder what else is still out there that Google doesn't know about
This is certainly not a first for Google, and we can only hope such a large-scale malicious operation is not to be repeated. A very concerning detail is that Videostrong was allowed to manufacture certified Android devices with Google apps. This means the company passed Google's required security testing that all hardware partners of the company have to go through.
Google says Videostrong used obfuscation to exploit a gap in those tests. The malicious code was designed to load only after the device's first boot — a sophisticated trick from the bad guys, indeed. At the same time, it's only natural to raise eyebrows at the questionable series of security and QC checks that failed to catch the malware for years. Checking what the firmware does after first boot should be a bare-minimum precaution. The whole purpose of a certificate is to assure buyers that someone has inspected what they are plugging into their TVs and using to sign in to their Google accounts.
Unfortunately, this is not an isolated weak point, and Google never fails to give us all a shock with news like this now and then. Very recently, Google promoted a fake Chrome app on its official store that showcased a six-figure download count despite copying the real browser's name, icon, and screenshots. While different, these two cases show how such threats can slip through Google-controlled security gates that users reasonably assume have already covered the basics.
Google now says it has cut ties with Videostrong and banned it from producing certified Android devices. It also says it has changed its review process to ensure nothing like this happens again. Google recommends purchasing set-top boxes only from reputable manufacturers that the company lists as official Android TV partners. While you're at it, Google, how about double-checking that list of certification holders, too?
Ordinary smart-TV privacy settings can reduce tracking without breaking major features, but they can't neutralize malware embedded in the firmware. Ideally, a certification should be more than boastful a logo on the packaging. Yet, Google’s security bolts were evidently not tight enough to catch something buyers had every reason to assume was being checked.
results.summary:
Google has dismantled a massive botnet involving 1.3 million Android set-top boxes manufactured by Videostrong, which contained preinstalled XCPE malware designed to facilitate ad fraud and data theft.

### Key Points
- The XCPE backdoor was embedded directly into the firmware of devices manufactured by Videostrong.
- Infected set-top boxes were used to conduct ad fraud, steal data, and route unauthorized traffic through users' home networks.
- Videostrong bypassed Google’s security certification by using obfuscation to trigger the malware only after the device's initial boot.
- Google has officially terminated its partnership with Videostrong and banned the company from producing certified Android devices.
- The tech giant has updated its security review processes to better detect malicious code hidden within device firmware.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights significant vulnerabilities in the supply chain for consumer electronics and raises concerns regarding the efficacy of Google’s hardware certification standards. It serves as a reminder that even officially certified devices can pose serious security risks, potentially compromising user privacy and home network integrity.

results.title: Funimation Shutdown Fuels Push for DMCA Exemption to Legally Rip Anime Content
results.author: Ernesto Van der Sar
results.content:
In April 2024, anime streaming service Funimation shut down its app and website, as it became part of Crunchyroll.
The closure also cut off access to the Funimation digital copies that came with DVDs and Blu-ray discs. This wasn’t well received by anime fans.
Today, Crunchyroll’s help page still states that it does not currently support these copies. Instead, the page encourages affected users to explore the anime streaming library that Crunchyroll does offer.
The movies and shows are still on the discs and in theory American buyers could make their own digital replacement copies. However, doing so would break the law as the DMCA’s anti-circumvention provision prohibits bypassing the encryption on DVDs and Blu-rays, unless an exemption applies.
Petitions Seek New Disc Ripping Exemption
The U.S. Copyright Office reviews these exemptions every three years, and last week it opened ten proposed classes for public comment. Two of the underlying petitions deal with works for which digital access was discontinued, and one specifically mentions the Funimation case.
One of these petitions comes from Jayden Milne. He asks the Office to allow owners of DVDs, Blu-ray and Ultra HD Blu-ray discs to make a single secured, local copy for personal use, when the digital copy promised on the packaging is no longer available.
That covers two situations. The first are people who redeemed a digital copy before the service behind it shut down, as happened with Funimation.
The second are buyers of new discs whose code had already expired. According to the petition, Warner Bros. states that its digital codes expire based on a title’s release date rather than the purchase date, and that expired codes are not replaced. This means that a disc bought years after its release may come with a code that no longer works.
Milne wants owners of these physical discs to be able to rip a replacement from them, under strict conditions.
The replacement can’t be better than what was promised. If the box offered an HD digital copy, for example, owners can’t rip the 4K version. Also, the copy is for personal use and it must be destroyed if the disc is sold, given away or lost.
Disappearing Anime Streams
A second and related petition, submitted by Zakaria Zerhouane, focuses on anime more broadly. It covers series and films that were removed from authorized U.S. streaming platforms after their licenses expired, as well as anime released on disc by U.S. distributors that no longer exist.
The petition does not mention Funimation but lists several distributors, including ADV Films, Bandai Entertainment, Central Park Media and Geneon.
In addition to bypassing encryption on discs, Zerhouane also wants to legally circumvent the DRM, geo-locking, and session-based access controls that streaming platforms use. This is needed, the petition argues, as the anime licensing market is unstable.
“Streaming platforms provide no advance removal notice, preventing users from finishing or preserving works before they disappear,” Zerhouane writes.
He adds that the consolidation of the U.S. anime market under “a single dominant entity” has made catalogs more volatile. The petition doesn’t name the company, but the description appears to fit Sony-owned Crunchyroll.
Neither petition covers all video content. Zerhouane’s request is limited to anime, while Milne’s only covers discs that came with a digital copy. Both petitions are restricted to personal and noncommercial uses.
Rightsholders Respond in February
The Copyright Office grouped these requests with four other ‘replacement’ petitions. These ask for personal backups of discs, including before they deteriorate, and permission to format-shift discs as playback hardware disappears. These become more relevant every year, as old formats decay.
The Office notes that the Register of Copyrights has repeatedly declined to recommend such format-shifting exemptions in the past. This means that, while they are on the agenda, approval is uncertain.
Before making any decision, the Office wants more details from stakeholders. It asks which copy protections are involved, whether the titles can be watched legally some other way, and why making these copies wouldn’t infringe copyright. It also wants to know whether allowing this would hurt sales.
Supporters have until December 7 to send in their comments. Opponents can respond until February 22, and public hearings will follow in the spring.
—
A copy of the Copyright Office’s notice of proposed rulemaking is available here (pdf). Jayden Milne’s petition can be found here (pdf), and Zakaria Zerhouane’s petition is available here (pdf).
results.summary:
The U.S. Copyright Office is reviewing petitions to allow consumers to legally bypass disc encryption for personal use after the Funimation streaming service shut down in April 2024.

### Key Points
- Funimation’s closure rendered digital copies included with physical media inaccessible, prompting consumer backlash and legal petitions.
- Petitioner Jayden Milne seeks an exemption to rip personal digital copies from discs when promised digital codes are expired or services are discontinued.
- Petitioner Zakaria Zerhouane requests legal circumvention of DRM and geo-locking for anime titles removed from streaming platforms due to expired licensing.
- The U.S. Copyright Office is currently accepting public comments on these proposed exemptions until December 7, with opposition responses due by February 22.
- Proposed rules would restrict personal copies to the quality originally promised and require their destruction if the physical disc is sold or lost.

### Why it Matters
These petitions highlight growing consumer frustration regarding the loss of digital access to purchased media following corporate consolidation and service shutdowns. A favorable ruling could set a significant precedent for digital ownership rights and the preservation of media in an increasingly volatile streaming market.

results.title: On Wall Street, the ‘energy transition’ includes natural gas and data centers
results.author: Austin Corona
results.content:
Blackstone, one of the largest private equity firms in the world, officially changed the name of its dedicated energy investment fund to include the phrase “energy transition” in 2022, having already ceased investing in oil and gas production five years earlier. The pivot toward a new energy future has not diminished interest in the fund. In mid-October, Blackstone announced that the fund pulled in $8.7 billion in investor money this year, reportedly turning away an additional $3 billion to stay under its maximum investment cap.
Blackstone’s is one of several energy transition funds at private equity firms that have consistently grown over the past decade. That growth has continued even as general climate-oriented investment has fallen over the last few years. Colloquially, “energy transition” refers to the shift from fossil fuels to renewable energy that is necessary to limit the worst impacts of climate change. But on Wall Street, the term can mean something a bit different. Some transition funds — including Blackstone’s — see opportunities for profit in natural gas, data centers, and rising electricity costs.
“I know a lot of the investors out there do consider gas a transition fuel,” said Ryan Loughead, a senior associate and former climate solutions analyst for BloombergNEF, an energy research firm.
Private equity funds take new investor money every few years and then use it to buy existing companies, maximize their profits, and then sell them, returning the money from the sale to investors. Unlike publicly traded companies, whose stocks are available for anyone to buy, private equity firms typically take investments only from large organizations, like pension funds, or very wealthy individuals, and they have faced criticism for prioritizing returns at the expense of workers and the environment.
The transition to renewable energy has been a booming business for private equity firms. “Transition funds” in private equity have raked in $178 billion between 2021 and the beginning of 2026, triple the amount raised by comparable funds dedicated to fossil fuels and general energy, according to Loughead’s research. They’ve maintained their popularity even as other forms of climate-related investments have flagged in the United States, with climate-related venture capital on track to suffer its worst year this decade. (While private equity funds buy out established companies, venture capital funds make smaller investments in startups.)
These shifts have coincided with changes in federal policy, as well as the overall economy. The Biden administration’s signature climate law once spurred innovation in new technologies, but Republicans in Congress repealed most of that legislation last year. Meanwhile, the tech industry’s data center buildout is creating surging demand for electricity and drawing trillions of dollars from investors.
In the financial industry, the energy transition has grown into a sophisticated economic trend with established players and markets, said Dan Cohn, an energy finance analyst with the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, a think tank focused on the energy transition. Private equity funds don’t typically demonstrate investor interest in a budding industry so much as a view that the industry is becoming economically important.
“Investors are sensing oncoming scarcity [of electricity] and are positioning themselves accordingly,” Cohn said. “That speaks to both the moment of rising electricity demand, but also the maturity of clean energy technologies.”
But while these funds seek to capitalize on high demand for electricity, they don’t all show a clear commitment to reducing emissions. Blackstone’s fund is explicit in its view that methane gas, a fossil fuel and the primary component of natural gas, is essential to the energy transition. The fund no longer invests in oil and gas fields, but it does invest in natural gas plants. When Blackstone rebranded it in 2022, the fund’s director, David Foley, explained why natural gas plants were still on the table. “A lot of the capital invested in the energy transition is going into simple renewable power generation assets like solar and wind,” he told an industry publication. “While this is important, just adding renewables to the grid doesn’t necessarily mean you can shut down and remove existing sources of power, such as coal and gas.”
This year, the fund announced investments in six companies, including a natural gas plant operator and a data center cooling technology company, alongside a company focused on renewable energy development and some transmission and grid technology companies. Blackstone did not reply to a request for comment.
Meanwhile, the private equity firm Brookfield governs its transition funds partly through an explicit commitment to decarbonization and emissions reductions. The company has said it can invest in natural gas in cases where it replaces dirtier fossil fuels, but Brookfield has also drawn criticism for describing gas expansion as part of the energy transition.
Similar funds in Europe, like Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners’ Energy Transition Fund, are far more focused on clean energy sources like green hydrogen, with little emphasis on natural gas.
“‘Energy transition’ is a flexible term,” Cohn said. “And I’m unsurprised to see either the gas or electrical equipment and data center-related companies in some of these funds. That is perfectly consistent with how I know some investors think about the energy transition.”
BlackRock, another private markets giant unrelated to Blackstone, explicitly defines “transition” investing as something different from “sustainable” investing: “not all sustainable strategies are transition, and not all transition strategies are sustainable,” its website reads.
That partial overlap could complicate investors’ claims about how sustainable their portfolios are.
At least three major government-managed investors in Blackstone’s energy transition fund have explicit climate investing goals. The Oregon Treasury, Minnesota State Board of Investment, and San Francisco Employees’ Retirement System all have some form of climate-related goal or plan for their investments. These entities have committed a combined $525 million to the fund, according to Private Equity International, an analytics firm.
These investors did not reply to requests for comment before publication of this article, but the wide range of standards for climate- and energy-related investments has already created confusion. In Oregon, a state representative formally asked the state’s treasury this year to more clearly define what it reports as “climate-positive” investments, which it uses as a category in its public reports.
Investors may have a financial incentive to include gas in their view of the energy transition. Transition funds that include gas tend to have slightly higher returns than those that don’t, Loughead said. And Loughead and Cohn both said the massive rush to invest in the data center boom has permeated funds nominally concerned with the clean energy transition.
Off Wall Street, the question of whether natural gas and data centers have a role to play in the energy transition is hotly debated. Natural gas has cut emissions from the power sector when it has replaced coal, while data centers have spurred investment in grid improvements and clean energy sources. But using natural gas still produces significant emissions — both when it’s burned and when it leaks out of infrastructure — and data centers are spurring more fossil fuel use, potentially slowing progress on global power sector emissions. Plus, some grids are already finding ways to provide reliability with cleaner alternatives to gas, like batteries, which can store renewable energy to use when the sun isn’t shining and the wind isn’t blowing. Most climate and environmental groups argue emphatically that gas should not be seen as a transition fuel.
“Natural gas no longer functions as a credible bridge in the energy transition,” wrote Shruti Shukla, a senior advocate on international energy at the Natural Resources Defense Council in a 2025 article, adding that the fuel “risks slowing decarbonization, raising system costs, and locking economies into avoidable volatility.”
And in the long run, it may not even come to be seen on Wall Street as a questionable investment, according to Cohn. As fuel price spikes continue driving the world toward renewables, fossil fuels may become less and less attractive as investment opportunities.
“There are other very prominent solutions like solar, wind, and batteries, which will mature and continue to see price declines, and so the view that you need gas is increasingly contested,” Cohn said.
This post has been updated to more accurately characterize the nature of BlackRock’s business.
results.summary:
Blackstone’s energy transition fund raised $8.7 billion this year, highlighting a growing trend where private equity firms prioritize profitable infrastructure like natural gas and data centers over renewables.

### Key Points
- Blackstone’s energy transition fund reached $8.7 billion in 2024, reportedly turning away $3 billion in additional investor capital.
- Private equity transition funds raised $178 billion between 2021 and early 2026, tripling the capital attracted by traditional fossil fuel and general energy funds.
- Blackstone’s strategy includes investments in natural gas plants and data center cooling technology, arguing that gas remains necessary for grid reliability.
- Major institutional investors, including the Oregon Treasury and Minnesota State Board of Investment, have committed $525 million to Blackstone’s fund despite varying climate goals.
- Analysts note that "energy transition" is a flexible term, with some firms prioritizing decarbonization while others focus on high-demand assets like natural gas and electricity infrastructure.

### Why it Matters
The broad definition of "energy transition" on Wall Street creates a disconnect between investor financial goals and environmental sustainability targets. As private equity firms increasingly bundle fossil fuel assets with clean energy, institutional investors face growing pressure to clarify whether these portfolios truly align with their stated climate commitments.

results.title: Wharton economist says his views on AI have 'radically shifted'
results.author: Ben Shimkus
results.content:
Sylvain Catherine loves his $200-a-month Claude — but he isn't convinced the race toward increasingly capable AI models is worth the risk.
The economist and associate professor of finance at The Wharton School recent made waves in the tech community when he declared on X that his "views on AI have radically shifted" after watching interviews with industry leaders and experts.
"I am deeply uncomfortable with the absolutely wild level of uncertainty around this prediction," he wrote on Sunday. "And to be honest, even setting the doom scenarios aside, I find the utopia scenarios of some industry leaders actually dystopian."
Catherine's post lands amid an ongoing debate over how to regulate AI's risks. AI skeptics like Gary Marcus applauded the post.
"Sanity is finally starting to win out," Marcus — who has been highly critical of AI companies and their business models — wrote in response.
On Monday, Business Insider's sister publication, POLITICO, reported that OpenAI's top policy executive is urging potential 2028 presidential candidates to develop a governing philosophy for AI, not just talking points. The memo obtained by the publication lays out questions including how society can share in the technology's benefits.
AI leaders themselves have offered wildly different visions of the technology's future. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has said AI could create so much abundance that money becomes useless; meanwhile, other leaders, like Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, have warned that AI could wipe out as much as 50% of entry-level white-collar work.
Catherine said there's still a range of possible outcomes. He said he believes that AI "can deliver significant increase to future GDP and help us solve major global challenges." His own Claude subscription, for example, is "worth every penny."
Catherine said his median prediction is that AI will slowly lift global GDP while stirring "some economic disruption" as employees find new kinds of work.
In a worst-case scenario, some tech leaders' visions for the future could be correct — namely, the forecast he finds "dystopian."
Catherine said he was surprised the industry had not faced more regulation, especially after OpenAI disclosed over the summer that agents in an internal cybersecurity evaluation escaped aspects of their testing environment and hacked into Hugging Face, an open-source platform.
Ultimately, he said there's one main solution for finding the right policy prescription for AI: sending Americans to the polls.
"A large majority of the public is now very skeptical of AI as a source of human progress, in particular among younger adults who use it the most," he said. "They should have a say."
results.summary:
Wharton finance professor Sylvain Catherine has expressed growing concern over the rapid development of artificial intelligence, citing extreme uncertainty and potential societal risks despite his personal use of tools.

### Key Points
- Sylvain Catherine, a finance professor at The Wharton School, publicly questioned the industry's trajectory, citing discomfort with both "doom" and "utopia" scenarios.
- OpenAI’s policy team is currently urging 2028 presidential candidates to establish formal governing philosophies regarding AI development and societal benefits.
