### Why it Matters
The debate highlights a growing divide between rapid technological advancement and the lack of comprehensive regulatory frameworks to manage economic and security risks. As AI integration accelerates, the pressure on policymakers to define governance strategies will likely become a central issue in future electoral cycles.

results.title: Your Apple Watch Can Automatically Identify Songs Around You
results.author: Tim Hardwick
results.content:
Ever been in a situation where you hear a song in a cafe, a shop, or a car, and wonder what it is? On the latest Apple Watch models, your watch can work it out for you, and you don't even need to ask. The music doesn't have to be playing on the watch. It just needs to be audible around you. Apple Watch does the rest.
It's all thanks to a new automatic feature in iOS 27 called Music Recognition, which is just one of Apple's new Audio Intelligence features. It uses Shazam to identify songs around you and surfaces the answer in the Smart Stack, including the title and artist, without you tapping anything. It requires an Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4 paired with an iPhone 11 or later (or iPhone SE 2nd generation or later) running iOS 27.
Using Music Recognition on Apple Watch
When you hear music nearby, just swipe up from the watch face (or turn the Digital Crown upward) to open the Smart Stack. Then check the Music Recognition widget. It should show the song title and artist as soon as it has identified the music, which shouldn't take long. The best bit is that you can save the song to your Shazam history or Apple Music library with a tap.
How to Turn On Automatic Music Recognition
Usually, you can just tap Enable Music Detection when the Music Recognition widget appears for the first time in your Smart Stack – the feature works from then on. But if for any reason you're not seeing it happen automatically after this initial step, here's how to enable it manually:
- Open the Settings app on your Apple Watch.
- Tap Smart Stack.
- Turn on Music Detection.
Older Apple Watch models can still identify songs manually with the Music Recognition app, but the automatic Smart Stack version is limited to Series 12 and Ultra 4.
Privacy
Apple says no audio is recorded or stored in the process of identifying songs. Instead, audio is processed in a protected buffer inside the device's Secure Exclave, and only an acoustic signature of the song – which can't be reversed into the original audio – is sent to Shazam's servers for identification.
results.summary:
Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 models now feature automatic music recognition, allowing users to identify songs playing in their environment directly through the device's Smart Stack.

### Key Points
- The new Music Recognition feature uses Shazam technology to identify songs without requiring manual input from the user.
- Automatic detection is exclusive to Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 devices paired with iPhones running iOS 27.
- Users can access identified song titles and artists by swiping up to view the Smart Stack widget.
- Identified tracks can be saved directly to a user's Shazam history or Apple Music library with a single tap.
- Apple processes audio through a protected buffer in the Secure Exclave, ensuring no actual audio recordings are stored or transmitted.

### Why it Matters
This update integrates advanced audio intelligence into the wearable ecosystem, streamlining how users discover and catalog music in real-time. By automating the identification process, Apple enhances the utility of the Smart Stack while maintaining strict privacy standards regarding user data.

results.title: The 4 Elements of Exposure Prioritization and How to Operationalize Them
results.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
results.content:
Your team is remediating more vulnerabilities than ever, yet your breach risk has barely changed. You’re spending too much time and effort on exposures attackers may never exploit, while higher-risk exposures sit, waiting in the queue. Gartner®’s report on exposure prioritization states that fewer than 10% of vulnerabilities are exploited, yet most are treated as urgent. The report also argues that CVSS scores alone do not predict actual exploitation or business impact.
Gartner predicts that by 2028, organizations that prioritize exposures using threat intelligence, asset context, exploitability modeling, and security control validation will reduce breach likelihood by at least 70% compared to their peers relying primarily on CVSS-based vulnerability prioritization. Let’s break down how each element works, and how the Picus Platform puts all four into practice.
Severity-based prioritization made sense. Then it didn't.
Severity-driven prioritization was an entirely rational response for the era it was built in: a static attack surface, scarce adversary tooling, and remediation capacity that exceeded disclosure volume. Suddenly, that world is gone. Enterprises face tens of thousands of new vulnerabilities a year across cloud, SaaS, identity, and supply chain modalities, and AI has compressed time-to-exploit from weeks or months to hours.
Gartner is candid about why teams still anchor on severity, and it’s not a lack of awareness. In fact:
- legacy metrics
- compliance pressure, and
- fragmented ownership
all reward what’s auditable over what’s legitimately impactful.
The result is widespread prioritization paralysis, with significant resources being funneled into remediation activity, but with remarkably little measurable risk reduction to show for it.
The smarter path is performing risk-based vulnerability management in its truest sense: measuring success by the exploitable exposures you’ve reduced, not the hypothetical vulnerabilities you’ve closed.
The four elements, and the question each one answers
Gartner’s framework rests on four pillars, and their value emerges only when added together. Sure, operationalizing one or two will bring you incremental gains, but integrating all four delivers significant reductions in both exposure windows and remediation fatigue.
Each element answers a distinct question about an exposure:
An exposure deserves urgent remediation only when all four answers converge.
The model aligns directly with the prioritization and validation stages of continuous threat exposure management (CTEM): remediation is mobilized only after priorities are validated in context.
Element 1: Threat Intelligence
Threat intelligence brings the adversary’s perspective into prioritization by showing which exposures attackers are actually exploiting. In real-world environments, many high-severity vulnerabilities are never exploited. Attackers frequently weaponize moderately rated vulnerabilities because they are easier to exploit, affect widely used systems, or can be exploited reliably. Past exploitation evidence helps teams focus their remediation efforts on a smaller, higher-risk subset of the backlog.
The operational challenge here is speed. Your team needs to use that intelligence to decide what to test and fix before a campaign reaches your environment. Track the time it takes to go from threat publication to testing and remediation.
Element 2: Asset Context and Business Criticality
An exploitable vulnerability becomes materially risky when it affects an asset that supports critical business functions, processes regulated data, or provides an easy pivot to higher-value systems. Without asset context, prioritization treats all assets as equal, and attention can easily drift to low-impact systems while crown-jewel exposures wait in the same queue.
This context already lives in tools most teams own: scanners, CMDBs, cloud security platforms, and identity systems. The practical work is to both unify it and keep it current, so its impact reflects the asset as it’s defended today, not as it appears in an inventory.
Element 3: Exploitability Modeling
Exploit prediction models such as EPSS estimate how likely a vulnerability is to be exploited, based on patterns like exploit complexity, component prevalence, and disclosure-to-exploitation timelines. These models complement threat intelligence by surfacing latent and lingering risks: helping identify the exposures that are statistically likely to be exploited before exploitation is widely observed, enabling you to shift teams from a reactive to an anticipatory or even proactive stance.
Statistical likelihood describes the world in general, not your organization’s unique environment. EPSS points to what’s probably exploitable somewhere; only validation proves what is exploitable here and now. Exploitability modeling works best as a filter that feeds validation, not as a final verdict.
Gartner’s full report goes deeper into how EPSS, KEV and similar models should be weighted against threat intelligence and control validation. Download the Gartner report on exposure prioritization to read the complete analysis.
Element 4: Security Control Validation
This is the element most programs are missing. Security control validation evaluates each exposure against the defenses already deployed around it: segmentation, endpoint protection, detection coverage, and identity controls.
An exposure that looks critical may be practically unreachable behind your existing defenses, while a less critical one on a poorly monitored asset may carry far more risk than its score suggests. Ignoring control context, Gartner warns, leads to systematic overestimation of risk and the wasted remediation efforts that follow it.
Testing shows whether attackers can realistically exploit an exposure in your specific environment today. Gartner notes this capability can be achieved with adversarial exposure validation techniques: proving exploitability with evidence, through live attack execution where testing is safe, and attack-chain analysis against deployed controls where assets can’t be touched.
How Picus Operationalizes All Four Elements into a Single Loop
The sum here is indeed greater than its parts, but the four elements only deliver their full value when evaluated together. This is, not surprisingly, where most organizations struggle as vulnerability management grows into exposure management. Why? Because in most organizations, threat intelligence sits with one team, asset context with another, exploitability scores are in a scanner, and control effectiveness only shows up in periodic assessments. Four inputs in four places do not lead to one decision.
Picus is named among the vendors in the 2026 Gartner® Market Guide for Adversarial Exposure Validation. The Picus Platform brings all four elements together in a continuous loop: Discover, Validate, Prioritize, and Mobilize.
Here’s how the platform maps to each element.
Security control validation deserves a closer look, because evidence is what turns the other three elements from assumptions into decisions. Picus Breach and Attack Simulation is one of three validation methods on the platform.
- Picus Autonomous Penetration Testing runs real exploit paths against reachable production assets and proves which ones lead to your critical systems.
- Picus Exposure Validation breaks each CVE into the techniques an attacker must use and tests every step against your existing controls on that asset, with no exploit fired, so even assets you can never test live get an evidence-backed verdict.
Together, these three validation methods give every exposure one explainable, organization-specific rating.
What Good Looks Like: Measuring the Shift
If prioritization is working, you should be able to see it in three places: your controls hold up better, you respond faster, and your team spends its time on the exposures that matter, rather than wasting it on the ones that don’t.
Here’s what our customers are reporting.
- Within three months of deploying Picus, their security controls are blocking or detecting roughly twice as many attacks as before.
- Response time to emerging threats drops by 89%.
- Missed remediation deadlines on high and critical vulnerabilities fall by 92%, because the queue now holds only the exposures proven to be exploitable.
One customer cut their critical ticket backlog by 98%. And the full cycle, from a new threat or change being detected to actual validated findings landing with the right team, runs under six hours.
A CISO at our 2026 Validation Summit put it simply: While a severity score is a useful label for sorting, the smarter strategy is to shut down those attack paths that could actually hurt your business. The numbers above back this up.
Exposure Prioritization Is a Risk Decision. Make It With Evidence.
Gartner frames exposure prioritization as a risk decision, and we agree.
Each of the four elements answers one part of it: threat intelligence tells you whether the exposure matters to an attacker, asset context tells you what it would cost you, exploitability modeling tells you how likely it is to take place, and security control validation tells you whether it could actually happen here.
The Picus Platform runs all four in one continuous loop, so every exposure ends in a decision you can defend to your board and your auditors: so you can fix it, mitigate it, or accept it with proof.
Ready to see validated prioritization in practice? Request a demo and watch one of your own CVEs go from a new scanner finding to the right response backed by evidence.
Note: This article was written by Sila Ozeren Hacioglu, Security Research Engineer at Picus Security.

By focusing resources on validated threats rather than hypothetical risks, organizations can significantly decrease their attack surface while reducing operational fatigue.

results.title: Radar Trends to Watch: November 2026
results.author: Mike Loukides
results.content:
Coauthored with Claude
Security looms large as we enter November. There’s been a lot of bad news: a certificate authority with woefully inadequate private keys, vulnerabilities have been discovered (and exploited) in PHP and other widely used programs, and several organizations have detected Chinese open weight models misbehaving in several different ways. New models are arriving faster and faster, and the best open-weight models are catching up to frontier model performance. But organizations that would like to achieve AI sovereignty will have to ask some difficult questions about the models they adopt. Is this an inflection point? Whether or not it is, AI has changed security permanently, and things are bound to get worse before they improve.
AI models
We are starting to see models developed with recursive self-improvement; we continue to see clones of Jev; and we’ve seen text watermarks added to output generated by Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s models. (Google has been using text watermarks for some time.) But tools for detecting the watermark are hard to find. Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s are in a very limited beta, and Google’s is only available in their enterprise package. What does a watermark mean if you can’t detect it? And, as we get more accustomed to AI-generated output, will anyone care?
- Kimi 3.1 Pro is a new open weight model with 3T tokens. On benchmarks, it is now the leading open weight model, only slightly behind the latest frontier models. Moonshot AI also released Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed, which is two to three times faster.
- Recursive has announced Flint, a 40B parameter mixture-of-experts model that activates 2.5B parameters per token. It was designed for coding, and sized to run on laptops. Flint is open weight; weights are available on Hugging Face, and it works with model runners like Ollama.
- Meta has shipped Muse Spark Open, an open weight model that they claim competes with the best Chinese open weight models. It’s a mixture-of-experts model with 816B parameters and 42B active parameters.
- Meta’s latest models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, claim parity with frontier-class models. Specifically, they claim parity with Claude and ChatGPT for financial and legal work. The announcement hints that Meta will be using Muse to develop specialized models.
- OpenAI’s Decisions API is yet another Jev-like model. Like Jev, its input is a data structure that constrains the model’s output to be an answer to specific questions. The output is a data structure that includes a probability for each answer.
- Claude has launched Haiku 5.5, a new version of its least expensive model. It’s faster, less expensive, and has better benchmark scores than its predecessors. Haiku 5.5 is a very capable model, particularly for users who are sensitive to cost.
- Mistral has launched Mistral Large 4, a.k.a Le Chonk. It’s an open weight mixture-of-experts model with 1T parameters. It’s claimed to be the best open model from Europe and was designed with AI sovereignty in mind.
- Aleph Alpha has released an open weight LLM for English and German that was trained entirely under European rules. It is a mixture-of-experts model with 78B parameters. It uses a different tokenizing algorithm to handle long German words without breaking them into fragments. Reasoning takes place mostly in German.
- Crowdflare has released Clef and Clef Flash, new decision models that, like Jev, take typed queries and return typed answers about those queries. It’s also offering a new reinforcement learning service to help customers train Clef for their applications.
- After a long wait, Google has released two new frontier models, Gemini 4 Argon and Carbon. Argon is available to paying customers. Argon’s successor, Carbon, is being released slowly, and is currently only available via the Fairwind program.
- The Ember-1 model from Fireworks claims to have results similar to Kimi K3 at lower costs. It is priced similarly on OpenRouter but uses far fewer reasoning tokens.
- OpenAI has published 722 papers solving problems in mathematics on GitHub. There is some controversy about whether all the proofs are correct; so far, three have been withdrawn, leaving 719.
- Google has opened its SynthID detector to the general public. The detector can determine whether audio, image, or video files generated by any of Google’s partners (including OpenAI, NVIDIA, and Apple) have the SynthID watermark.
- To comply with EU law, OpenAI will add watermarks to text in Europe. The company’s algorithm sounds similar to the one that Google and Anthropic are using: modifying the underlying probability distribution changes word choice in detectable but insignificant ways.
Agents and harnesses
There are more choices than ever for agents, along with new standards for the interaction between agents and models. In addition to general purpose agents, there are also agents specialized for coding, HR, BI, and more. And most agents will connect to many models, including local ones. Choose agents as carefully as you choose models; your agent is where you will do your work.
- JetBrains has released Thinkrail, an agentic IDE that learns about your project as you use it. It is open source and based on the pi agent.
- Anthropic has donated its Agent Skills standard to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF), which will shepherd further development. It has also donated Open Responses, a standard for building common interfaces, to AI providers.
- OpenAI has introduced Intelligent UI, a feature that allows ChatGPT to generate its own user interfaces in response to the user’s question.
- Workday is allowing its customers to build their own agents for HR and finance. An agent’s access to Workday data is tied to the user’s account.
- Claude Dashboards is a new product that lets you build live dashboards from a group of data sources.
- Claude’s Google Workspace connectors allow it to read and write Google documents, sheets, and slides directly.
- MCP Events is an extension to the MCP protocol from OpenAI. It allows ChatGPT to subscribe to updates from MCP servers.
- DeepSeek has released a harness (dsh). It’s open source, and currently in public preview. Everything is a plug-in.
- The Pi agent has reached version 1.0.0, and is now capable of using MCP. There’s a variation, Pi Durable, that has been designed for long-running tasks.
- OpenAI dots are consumer-oriented agents that run in the cloud. They are always on and have their own web browser along with other tools.
Software development
At last month’s SciFoo, Hugo Bowne-Anderson said that we’ve been through two major changes in the past few years: from writing code to letting AI write the code, and from reading the code to not reading the code. These changes are as radical as the shift from programming in machine language to programming in high-level languages. We will all go through a process of rethinking how we work and what we’re trying to accomplish.
- Anthropic has introduced Claude Mods, a plug-in for Claude Code that can modify Code’s behavior: reshaping its user interface, providing information about context use, giving advice about what you’re doing, and much more.
- One application for decision models is building evals to understand the performance of AI applications.
- Workday is using Jev to build user interfaces on the fly. Jev’s very low latency makes choosing UI components at runtime viable.
- Anthropic has outgrown Git, which wasn’t able to keep up with merges on their monorepo (roughly 30,000 merges in September). Anthropic has built a new source control system called Scion.
- Kate Huston writes about reverse-engineering code review and trying to develop an effective “gate” that AI-generated code would have to pass before review by humans.
- WordCraft is an open source clean-room re-implementation of Microsoft Word. The authors claim that it’s 60% of the way towards “replacing Word for real work.” It supports MCP, has a command line interface for interacting with agents, and can run in a browser through WASM.
- ArtCraft is an open source tool for creating interactive AI-generated images and video in 2D or 3D. The company describes it as an “IDE for artists.” They’re also developing open source clones of Adobe Creative Suite tools like Photoshop. Early reports are that it’s very buggy.
- Google Docs now supports Markdown natively. Users can read, write, collaborate, and comment on Markdown documents without converting them to another format.
- Google’s Docsy documentation project is moving to the Linux Foundation. Docsy is a template for the Hugo static site generator that’s useful for generating documentation in ways that are helpful to agents.
- Does programming with AI require more abstractions or fewer? Matt Pocock argues for more.
- Anthropic has given Claude an auto-eval tool. While the first version of this tool has many flaws, it’s a significant step towards making evals easier.
Security
Security has been much in the news. Not all of the news is bad: AI was used to discover the PHP2Shell vulnerability and to develop a fix. The leaked CVE and the many out-of-date PHP sites online are serious problems, but not problems attributable to AI. Too many problems arise from getting the basics wrong: A certificate authority using 4 as its private key is a mistake that should never have been made. As always, security is about getting the basics right while watching for new threats. And while organizations claim to be paying more attention to security, the word from insiders is that “attention” means lip service. In the long run, AI may make the world a safer place, but the next few years look scary.
- CrowdStrike and Booz Allen have found that Qwen3-Coder (and probably other models) generates weaker code if the prompt says that the code is for a politically sensitive user such as the US government. Hirundo reports similar flaws and also claims to have “fixed” the model and created a Westernized version.
- Cohere makes a different claim: It has observed that Qwen3.8 models occasionally send data to an Alibaba cloud storage bucket in Beijing.
- Malicious AGENTS.md files have been found in the Downloads folders of some users. If the user is using the Downloads folder as their working directory, an AI agent will read the AGENTS file and download a malicious NPM package.
- 1Password has launched 1Password for Agents, a credential-brokering product that allows agents to access resources for a user without seeing the user’s password,
- Alibaba also donated its OpenSandbox project to AAIF. OpenSandbox is a general-purpose sandbox for running AI models safely.
- The PHP team has released patches for two critical vulnerabilities collectively known as PHP2Shell. However, many sites are running old versions of PHP that need to be upgraded before they can be patched. The maintainers have also released some partial mitigations for sites that can’t upgrade easily, but that won’t fully protect them. Sadly, “the panic hasn’t turned into patching,” and those who don’t patch will pay.
- Brotli isn’t as widely used as PHP, or as old, but a critical flaw in Brotli compression library makes it clear that discovery of hidden vulnerabilities is the shape of things to come. Microsoft has released patches for .Net, PHP maintainers have released patches for PHP, Node.js is also affected, and that’s just the start.
- The private keys of the certificate authority eMudhra have been cracked–not by brilliant cryptography or a quantum computer, but because the keys were generated very poorly. The Chrome and Firefox browsers aren’t trusting the compromised certificates, but almost everything else, including all major package managers, is a problem.
- OpenCode was the victim of a hostile attack in which some users’ API keys and passwords were stolen from their Console service. Its response was hampered by lack of access to AI models without security restrictions.
- The US Department of Homeland Security has banned the use of DeepSeek and applications developed using DeepSeek in all federal agencies.
- To monitor the risks created by the development of frontier models, Anthropic has given six employees of METR access to their models. They continue to work with Accenture and Secure Bio.
- Model abliteration is a poisoning attack in which post-training is used to discover which of a model’s weights corresponds to “no,” and altering them so the model cannot refuse a request. It’s effectively a backdoor into the model’s behavior.
- AWS has launched Strands Box, an open source sandbox that’s designed specifically to prevent AI agents from escaping the sandbox’s control. It includes an open source policy engine, Dogwood, that allows users to place explicit limits on what an agent may do.
- Meta’s Muse, its agent for people who aren’t technology professionals, is a privacy and security disaster.
- Using MCP for communications between agents creates many risks, including new vulnerabilities to prompt injection.
- Google has suspended submissions to the Open Source Software Vulnerability Rewards Program because of the flood of machine-generated vulnerability reports, most of which are (in Google’s words) “not valid.” This suspension should only be temporary.
Infrastructure and operations
There’s been a lot of news about certificate management, not all of it good. It’s time to check on your certificate providers, get ready for quantum-resistant encryption, and automate as much of the process as you can.
- To increase security, the certificate provider Let’s Encrypt will be limiting the lifetime of free certificates to 64 days starting in February 2027. The change should be invisible to sites using automatic certificate management (ACME).
- Crowdflare has announced that it will begin issuing TLS certificates with quantum-resistant encryption. They will continue issuing certificates with classical encryption. Crowdflare hasn’t given a date when they will start issuing the new certificates.
- DeepSeek has open sourced DeepInfer, its inference framework, with an Apache 2.0 license. At present, DeepInfer only supports DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash.
- RemoveMacAI is an open source command-line tool for deleting Apple’s AI from MacOS 27, freeing up 30 GB or so of disk space.
Web
Mark Twain didn’t quite say, “The reports of my death are greatly exaggerated.” But we are hearing that the Web is dead, and that’s indeed an exaggeration. The flood of crawler traffic and the disincentives towards human writing are a problem. But what does “death” mean for a technology so flexible that you can build an office suite that stores entire documents’ URLs?
- TinyLittleOffice.com is a surprisingly complete set of surprisingly capable office applications. It includes a word processor, spreadsheets, and other Office-like apps. Everything is saved in the URL–not on your disk, not in someone’s datacenter. Not suitable for large documents.
- Crowdflare has announced a web search API, now in beta. Although their announcement doesn’t say, we suspect this is an attempt to control web scraping traffic. Matthew Prince, its CEO, has estimated that bot traffic will reach 1000 times human traffic by mid-2027. All of his earlier predictions have been underestimates.
- Jev and its clones have taken the world by storm. Can you beat it at Pacman?
Hardware
- AI labs are heading towards models that can run on phones and similar hardware. Google has compressed Gemma 4 E4B to 5 GB, and Liquid has released LFM2.5-24B-A2B, a 24B mixture-of-experts model with 2B active parameters that also targets devices.
- OpenTPU is an open source API accelerator, designed by AI. Bring your own silicon.
Quantum computing
- Quantinuum has implemented quantum error correction on its latest hardware and has found that it scales well enough to be useful in practice: Adding a physical qubit to a logical cubit cuts the error rate significantly.
- Researchers have discovered a way to read a qubit without collapsing the information it contains into a 1 or 0. Solving this problem (also known as quantum non-demolition or QND) is critical to building quantum computers large enough to do useful work.
Biology
- Watermarking texts is one thing. Google has now designed a watermark for proteins. Like text watermarks, protein watermarks are based on Google’s SynthID.
- Last month we mentioned EEG-capable earbuds. This month, a group of researchers has announced that they have developed an AI application that can reconstruct what someone is seeing from brain scans. The results are impressive, though the privacy implications are chilling.
results.summary:
The rapid evolution of AI models and agentic tools is reshaping software development and cybersecurity, introducing both advanced capabilities and significant new vulnerabilities for organizations to manage.

### Key Points
- New open-weight models like Kimi 3.1 Pro, Mistral Large 4, and Meta’s Muse series are achieving performance parity with frontier-class AI systems.
- Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google are expanding AI agent standards and interfaces, including the Agent Skills standard and ChatGPT’s Intelligent UI feature.
- Security threats are escalating, highlighted by the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, compromised eMudhra certificate authority keys, and malicious AI agent activity.
- Google has expanded its SynthID watermarking technology to include protein structures, while OpenAI prepares to implement text watermarking to comply with EU regulations.
- The US Department of Homeland Security has banned the use of DeepSeek models across all federal agencies due to emerging security and data privacy concerns.

### Why it Matters
The integration of AI into critical infrastructure and development workflows is creating a complex security landscape where traditional defenses are increasingly insufficient. Organizations must balance the rapid adoption of powerful new models and agents with rigorous security protocols to mitigate risks like prompt injection, data leakage, and supply chain attacks.

results.title: We have the most powerful technology in history, and we’re using it to stop hiring young people
results.author: Mark Minevich
results.content:
We hold the most powerful technology in human history, and so far corporate America is mostly using it to write marketing copy and cut headcount.
Through September, U.S. employers announced 573,195 job cuts. Artificial intelligence was cited in 120,136 of them, more than any other reason this year, according to outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas. Tech companies alone announced 165,925 cuts, up 54% from the same period last year.
To be fair, total announced cuts are down 39% from the first nine months of 2025, and AI was cited in only about 9% of September’s cuts. The bigger effect is on hiring. Using ADP payroll data, Stanford economists Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen found that as of June, employment among 22- to 25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed occupations was about 19% below where it would be if it had kept pace with young workers in less-exposed jobs. A year earlier, the gap was 15%. They write that the adjustment works “primarily through reduced hiring of young workers rather than increased separations.”
Companies aren’t firing junior workers; they are simply not hiring them. They’re using efficiency as the excuse.
A great economy for whom?
On paper, the economy looks powerful. Real GDP grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter, up from 2.2% in the second, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis. Spending on computer equipment, a soft landing for capital expenditure, was a main driver.
But for the common citizen, this year has been anything but a soft landing. Consumer prices rose 3.7% in the year through September, and gasoline rose about 34%. Since the Iran war closed the Strait of Hormuz in March, oil has gone through what the World Bank calls “the largest oil market shock in history.”
In addition, workers now pay an average of $7,471 a year toward family health coverage, up 9% from 2025, according to KFF. Over roughly the same period, wages increased only 3.7%. Effectively, the people took a pay cut.
The looming electricity and water crises
The AI buildout is also competing with households for the same electricity. In PJM, the largest U.S. grid operator, the independent market monitor estimated that data centers caused 63% of the price increase in 2025/2026, about $9.3 billion in costs, according to the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis. Pepco residential customers in Washington, D.C., saw bills rise about $21 a month starting in June 2025. Roughly $10 of that came from capacity prices.
This is what makes me angry. None of these issues requires new technology to be solved. The models exist, the compute exists, and the capital is already being spent. What’s missing is a decision about where to point it.
The American Society of Civil Engineers estimates a water main breaks every two minutes in the U.S., and about 6 billion gallons of treated water is lost daily. We could use AI to forecast load and balance the grid so data centers pay for the strain they add. We could use AI to find leaks in water systems. We could model drought before it reaches a farm, inspect bridges, harden supply chains, and cut diagnosis costs instead of raising premiums.
In June, in the U.K., Northumbrian Water reported that a six-month trial using AI-powered acoustic sensors to help crews locate hidden leaks was saving nearly 6.4 million liters of water a day. This is the technology we must invest in and deploy immediately.
San Jose Water installed 13,600 fixed acoustic sensors across its 2,400-mile network, and the system found 483 leaks and saved more than 400 million gallons of treated water. Plus, New Mexico’s LeakTracer satellite-plus-AI program identified 216 leaks across 181 miles of pipe in its first year. Completing the needed repairs could recover 328 million gallons and save about $505,000 a year.
This must become the industry standard.
Four steps to secure the future
First, we must treat energy resilience as a national security issue. Data centers must be required via litigation to pay for the grid upgrades and capacity they drive. Families shouldn’t have to subsidize the infrastructure required by multibillion-dollar tech companies. AEP Ohio already requires new data-center customers to reimburse 100% of buildout costs if they cancel before energization. The company creating the demand, carrying the risk, must be fundamental.
In my home state, New Jersey’s Data Center Fair Share Act was signed in July 2026, creating a separate rate class for large data centers. This requires them to cover their own infrastructure costs, demands financial guarantees covering at least 85% of requested load for 10 years, and lets them offset capacity obligations by paying for demand reductions elsewhere. This could save ratepayers more than $1 billion a year. Other states are moving in the same direction, with large-load tariffs imposing high minimum-demand charges and contribution-in-aid rules so residential customers aren’t charged if a project underdelivers or exits.
Next, go after health costs at the source. Use AI to reduce the volume of unnecessary tests, procedures, and late-stage interventions rather than simply shifting higher premiums onto households. Start by capping excessive hospital prices in public employee health plans, with safeguards for vulnerable hospitals. Oregon capped in-network hospital payments at twice Medicare’s rates and saved an estimated $107.5 million over 27 months. Then require publicly funded health care AI projects to demonstrate lower costs without compromising care. Efficiency isn’t helping if the patient’s bill remains the same.
Third, deploy AI to retrain people faster than it replaces them. By tying public incentives for AI investment and data-center build-out to measurable entry-level hiring and apprenticeship commitments, AI will create efficiency and jobs. As entry-level roles disappear for the benefit of only AI owners, the coming generations are being steered toward economic ruin. Tie public AI incentives to net-new paid apprenticeships and entry-level jobs, with payments after six and 12 months of verified employment and not simply after a training course.
This isn’t some pipe dream; the blueprint exists. In July, the Labor Department awarded nearly $162 million through an apprenticeship program that links payments to verified retention and progression milestones. Reward employers for being job creators and builders. Going forward, any firm receiving tax credits, accelerated permitting, or public power-purchase support for AI capacity must fund or host a proportional number of paid apprenticeships or entry-level roles, with progress reported publicly.
Finally, give public infrastructure the same AI investment private data centers get. One of the most impactful improvements AI could make is in utilities and water. As governments embed AI into power grids and water systems to stabilize national infrastructure, we should use AI-driven material evaluation of roads and highways and continuous monitoring to predict repair needs before learning from injuries and accidents. Funding can be mandated by dedicating a share of data-center tax revenue to local infrastructure technology. Virginia began taxing data-center electricity consumption at 1.1 cents per kilowatt-hour in July. States should direct a portion of that revenue toward leak detection, grid management, and bridge inspection, plus paying the employees who act on the findings.
A dedicated public AI infrastructure fund can be created and financed by a small, transparent tax on large data-center power or compute capacity, matched by federal and philanthropic capital.
When voters go to the polls Tuesday, they won’t vote on GDP. They’ll vote on whether things at home got easier or harder since their last ballot was dropped in the box. With AI, the question isn’t whether we can point this technology at the problems that decide whether people can afford to live and create a solution. We can do that. The real question is whether anyone in charge is willing to, or if they just want to keep eliminating the future of work for the next generations.

results.summary:
U.S. employers are increasingly using artificial intelligence to reduce hiring and cut costs, prompting calls for policy reforms to protect infrastructure, healthcare affordability, and entry-level job opportunities.

### Key Points
- Challenger, Gray & Christmas reported that AI was cited in 120,136 of the 573,195 U.S. job cuts announced through September.
- Stanford economists found that hiring for 22- to 25-year-olds in AI-exposed occupations is 19% lower than in less-exposed sectors.
- Data centers are driving significant electricity price hikes, with the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis estimating they caused $9.3 billion in grid costs.
- Successful AI deployments in water management, such as San Jose Water’s sensor network, have saved hundreds of millions of gallons of treated water.
- New Jersey’s Data Center Fair Share Act and Oregon’s hospital price caps serve as legislative models for mitigating the economic impact of AI and rising costs.

### Why it Matters
The current deployment of AI is prioritizing corporate efficiency and headcount reduction over public infrastructure stability and workforce development. Without policy intervention, the concentration of resources in data centers and the displacement of junior workers threaten long-term economic mobility and the affordability of essential utilities for households.

results.title: Microsoft made Windows 11 more responsive on these 8GB laptops
results.author: c.cale.hunt@gmail.com (Cale Hunt) , Cale Hunt
results.content:
Microsoft has been busy at work reducing the amount of RAM that Windows 11 consumes, and it finally made an official statement today on the topic.
As it turns out, the company has already been quietly shipping performance improvements in the latest Windows 11 updates, focusing on making systems with 8GB of RAM feel a lot more responsive.
The result? Microsoft says Windows 11 is now about 20% more responsive on 8GB PCs compared to before this work started. The work also applies to systems with 4GB, 16GB, and beyond, with specific tuning for each amount.
This couldn't come at a better time. RAM and storage shortages (explained below) are driving up the cost of all PCs, and models with 8GB of RAM are being revived to lessen the burden on consumers.
Our favorite 8GB Windows laptops in November 2026
Why you can trust Windows Central
Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
Companies like Dell, Acer, and HP have all recently launched 8GB laptops that cost somewhere around $699, with student and regular discounts frequently dropping those numbers lower.
If you were hesitant to shop for an 8GB laptop before, the recent Windows 11 updates should have you reconsidering, especially when prices are this reasonable. Here are my three favorite 8GB laptops right now.
Dell's awesome XPS 13 starts at $699.99 (or $599.99 if you're a student) and includes an Intel Core 5 320 CPU, 8GB of LPDDR5x RAM, a 256GB M.2 PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD, and a 13.4-inch touch display with 2560x1600 resolution
Dell's new XPS 13 for 2026 wowed both Zac Bowden and me at Computex earlier this year, and it's been available to buy since June.
It's a laptop with many premium features despite its price, including a higher-res 2560x1600 (QHD+) display with a 120Hz refresh rate, an IR camera for Windows Hello facial recognition, capable speakers, and a comfortable keyboard/touchpad combo.
It does not, however, offer USB-A or 3.5mm audio ports. Its display does not use an OLED panel; it uses IPS instead. And the $599 price is only available for students.
Still, $699 for everyone else is not bad at all in this economy, and most users should have no issues with the XPS 13.
HP's 14-inch OmniBook 5 is currently on sale for $599.99. It has an Intel Core 5 320 CPU, 8GB of LPDDR5x RAM, a 256GB M.2 PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD, and a 14-inch OLED touch display with 1920x1200 resolution.
HP's OmniBook 5 14 comes with the same Intel Core 5 320 CPU as the other laptops in this roundup, so don't expect any major performance changes.
The OmniBook 5 includes an OLED panel for deeper contrast and more vivid color than IPS. The tradeoff is a lower 1920x1200 resolution and lower 60Hz refresh rate compared to the XPS 13.
HP's laptop also includes HDMI and 3.5mm audio ports alongside dual USB-C at 10Gbps. It's nice to have native video, but the lack of Thunderbolt is a letdown.
This laptop is currently on sale for $599.99 for everyone, making it (temporarily) the best deal of the bunch.
Acer's Swift Air 14 immediately makes an argument for itself with twice as much storage (512GB) as the Dell and HP laptops. For those who prefer to store locally, this could be the deciding factor. However, it does drop down to PCIe 3.0 speeds.
Performance is largely the same thanks to it having the Intel Core 5 320 chip inside, with 8GB of LPDDR5x RAM.
The display hits a 1920x1200 resolution; it doesn't have touch, but it does hit a smoother 120Hz refresh rate. You're definitely giving up some screen quality to land that extra storage.
While the keyboard is great, the touchpad leaves something to be desired. Your experience may vary.
Why is Microsoft concerned with reducing Windows 11 RAM usage?
Sure, Windows 11 could always be more streamlined, but this big push for more RAM efficiency is also a result of the ongoing memory and storage crisis.
See, AI data centers are eating up many of the foundational components of PCs, making the consumer side far more expensive.
RAM in particular has exploded in price; the same 32GB kit of DDR5 I bought for my gaming PC a few years ago, for example, is roughly 600% more expensive today. Storage isn't much better.
This is forcing PC makers to reevaluate their product lineups, as many consumers can no longer afford PCs with 16GB or more of RAM.
Cutting RAM in half is a huge cost saver and won't likely stop anytime soon (the RAM crisis could last for years to come), so it's great to see Microsoft taking user complaints about Windows 11's responsiveness (or lack thereof) seriously.
Join us on Reddit at r/WindowsCentral to share your insights and discuss our latest news, reviews, and more.
Cale Hunt brings to Windows Central more than nine years of experience writing about PC gaming, Windows laptops, accessories, and beyond. If it runs Windows or in some way complements the hardware, there’s a good chance he knows about it, has written about it, or is already busy testing it.
results.summary:
Microsoft has optimized Windows 11 to improve system responsiveness by 20% on devices with 8GB of RAM, helping maintain performance amid rising global hardware and memory costs.

### Key Points
- Microsoft updated Windows 11 to enhance efficiency for systems with 4GB, 8GB, and 16GB of RAM.
- The performance improvements aim to mitigate the impact of rising component costs driven by high demand for AI data centers.
- Major manufacturers including Dell, HP, and Acer are currently offering 8GB laptops priced between $599 and $699.
- Specific models highlighted include the Dell XPS 13, HP OmniBook 5, and Acer Swift Air 14, all featuring Intel Core 5 320 processors.

### Why it Matters
These optimizations allow budget-conscious consumers to maintain a smooth computing experience on entry-level hardware despite the ongoing global memory and storage crisis. By reducing the resource footprint of Windows 11, Microsoft is helping PC manufacturers keep affordable 8GB laptops viable in a market where high-end memory prices have surged.

results.title: Google Drops the Hammer: What the Videostrong Scandal Means for Your Streaming Boxes
results.author: Andrew Allen
results.content:
If you have a Mecool smart TV box plugged into your living room setup, a recent bombshell announcement from Google and its Threat Intelligence Group demands your attention. Google recently dismantled a massive, global cybercrime operation, dubbed the “XCPE botnet” that turned over 1.3 million consumer devices into secret spy and ad-fraud gadgets.
At the center of this massive security breach is a hardware manufacturer called Videostrong, and its popular consumer-facing subsidiary, Mecool. For the average consumer, corporate terms like “botnets” and “firmware backdoors” can sound intimidating. However, understanding what went wrong is critical to keeping your home network safe.
What Did Videostrong Do?
According to Google’s detailed technical report, hardware maker Videostrong deliberately embedded a hidden backdoor (the XCPE malware) directly into the core system software of its devices over a period of years.
Instead of a typical hacker breaking into a device after purchase, this threat was built right into the factory code. Videostrong allegedly used this hidden access to monetize the devices behind the owners’ backs. They sold remote access to criminal groups, turning everyday living room boxes into tools for:
- Residential Proxy Networks: Selling your home internet bandwidth to unknown third parties (using modules like Linkfog, AppSalt, NetNut, and GaGaNode) so traffic could be routed through your IP address.
- Ad-Fraud Engines: Quietly running background applications with transparent window overlays and hidden WebViews to simulate human web traffic, clicks, and video views to steal advertising money.
- Deep Surveillance: Granting operators the ability to capture live screenshots, inject keystrokes, execute shell commands, and exfiltrate system logs and sensitive device data.
How Does This Affect the Mecool Subsidiary and Everyday Users?
For everyday shoppers, Mecool is the most widely recognized brand tied to Videostrong. Mecool manufactures popular Android TV set-top boxes frequently bought online for streaming.
Because of these severe infractions, Google has taken swift, definitive action:
- The Death Penalty for the Brand: Google has permanently banned Videostrong—along with any of its subsidiaries, partners, and future affiliates (including Mecool)—from building or selling certified Android devices, or supplying software to other certified vendors.
- Compromised Hardware: Security firms analyzing the fallout note that many popular Mecool-branded boxes were shipped with this backdoor pre-installed.
- The Hard Truth for Owners: Because the malware runs as a system-level application signed with the manufacturer’s own keys, security experts warn that average users cannot remove it. If you clear the system or factory reset the device, the malware automatically reinstalls itself from the core firmware.
What Should You Do Next?
If you own a Mecool streaming box or a generic Android TV box linked to Videostrong, cybersecurity experts recommend treating the device as completely compromised. The safest course of action is to unplug the device, disconnect it from your network, and safely dispose of it. Additionally, it is wise to change your home Wi-Fi password to clear out any lingering digital access.
Google’s decisive shutdown is a major win for internet safety, but it serves as a stark reminder: always buy smart home tech from trusted, mainstream brands with proven track records for supply-chain security.
results.summary:
Google has permanently banned hardware manufacturer Videostrong and its subsidiary Mecool after discovering a pre-installed backdoor that turned 1.3 million Android TV boxes into a global botnet.

### Key Points
- Google’s Threat Intelligence Group dismantled the XCPE botnet, which utilized hidden firmware backdoors to facilitate ad fraud and residential proxy services.
- The malware allowed unauthorized third parties to capture screenshots, log keystrokes, and execute shell commands on compromised devices.
- Videostrong and its subsidiary, Mecool, are now prohibited from producing or supplying certified Android devices.
- Security experts state the malware is embedded in the core firmware, making it impossible for users to remove via factory resets.
- Owners of affected Mecool streaming boxes are advised to disconnect the devices from their networks and dispose of them immediately.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights significant supply-chain security risks when purchasing smart home hardware from less-regulated manufacturers. Consumers should prioritize established brands to avoid devices that may compromise home network privacy and security through pre-installed malicious software.

results.title: 2026 Hackaday Supercon: Bruce Potter’s Keynote Explores the Hacker Mind
results.author: Tom Nardi
results.content:
What is hacking? Many, especially in the mainstream, view it through the lens of computer security. Others consider it synonymous with making or creating. Even for those of us immersed in the community, this can be a surprisingly difficult question to answer.
In his Hackaday Supercon 2026 keynote address, Bruce Potter will explore this idea by taking a step back and looking at what makes someone a hacker in the first place. Rather than viewing hacking as a singular act, he’ll make the case that it’s a mindset, a way of approaching problems that’s not strictly dependent on the tools used or even the desired outcome.
With a cybersecurity career that’s spanned three decades, Bruce has been involved with hacking at every level and in every form — from conducting DARPA research to founding The Shmoo Group and helping organize the legendary ShmooCon. Currently the Chief Product Officer at Trinity Cyber, Bruce has made creative problem solving his life’s work, and he’s eager to share what he’s learned with the Hackaday community. While most of us won’t get the opportunity to advise on national cybersecurity policy as he has, we can still apply the same techniques to our own personal and professional projects.
Those joining us this weekend in Pasadena will get to experience Bruce’s keynote, as well as more than 30 other fascinating presentations, with a group of individuals who are just as eager to understand the how and why of the world around them as you are. Making personal connections with like-minded folks is truly the highlight of Hackaday Supercon; badge hacking and tacos are just the fringe benefits.
In our totally unbiased opinion, we believe Hackaday Supercon is the ultimate hardware hacking conference, but you don’t have to take our word for it. A few tickets are still left if you want to see for yourself.
