Cybersecurity expert Bruce Potter will deliver the keynote address at the 2026 Hackaday Supercon in Pasadena, exploring the core mindset and creative problem-solving philosophy behind modern hacking.

### Key Points
- Bruce Potter, Chief Product Officer at Trinity Cyber, will headline the 2026 Hackaday Supercon event.
- The keynote focuses on defining hacking as a versatile mindset rather than a specific set of technical tools.
- Potter’s career includes three decades of experience, ranging from DARPA research to co-founding the ShmooCon security conference.
- The weekend event in Pasadena features over 30 presentations centered on hardware hacking and collaborative engineering.
- Limited tickets remain available for attendees interested in the conference's technical workshops and community networking opportunities.

### Why it Matters
This keynote highlights the evolution of hacking from a narrow security focus to a broader methodology for creative problem-solving in professional and personal projects. By framing hacking as a mindset, the event encourages engineers and hobbyists to apply these analytical techniques to diverse technical challenges.

results.title: I use AI (Oct 2026)
results.author: Ben Stolovitz
results.content:
How I use AI (Oct 2026)
Wow, things have changed.
Last October, I took stock of how I was using AI — specifically the cool stuff like LLMs that we call 'AI’. I’m so glad I did. Things are very, very different 12 months later.
Background
I still believe I use AI fairly typically, but I’ve had a notable change in background. Last October, I was an engineer on Microsoft’s Windows AI team. I am now a research engineer at Salesforce AI Research. I spend more time supporting scientists & building rapid prototypes, rather than working with a large team of engineers. I spend about ~$3,000/month in tokens.
In any case, I mostly use AI in the same ways as last year:
- Coding
- Research & search
- Summarization & transcription & (new) voice
- Writing
- Art & music & (new) video
Also new this year, I’ve drafted a personal AI policy; we’ll start there.
As before, this remains purely my opinion & speculation. If you use AI differently, let me know!
My AI policy
This year I began drafting a personal AI policy — as in, a document for how I want to use AI in my life. I am very excited about it. I am also working on an explicit AI policy for this site (still thinkin’; probably based on Hank Green’s policy), but a personal policy is to give me a framework for using these tools day-to-day.
AI leaks into life. Teammates ask Claude to write their Slack messages, grandparents generate creepy memes of their grandchildren, and researchers delegate their thinking to machines. I’ve seen all of these things; even strong creators like Hank Green and BrainPOP get lost.
Humans clearly do not have norms for using these tools, and we’re messing up. I hope that a personal policy will ground me as AI becomes smarter. I hope to adapt that policy over time, and I’m eager to see how it evolves. I’m also open to draft 1 being utterly, hopelessly wrong.
Ultimately, I want to spend my life making cool things with other people. AI can help, AI can hurt. A policy helps me find the difference.
Coding
Writing code is solved.
Last year, I waxed poetic about how GitHub Copilot autocomplete transformed how I write code.
Well, uh, I no longer write much code. Agentic coding has made it obsolete.
My workday now means managing ~5–6 Claude Code (or OpenCode or Codex or Pi) agents. I’ll give Claude a feature to implement, or a bug to reproduce, or any other task I used to do by hand; each agent gets its own copy of the code (a Git worktree, if you’re technical), then just… gets to work. The agents write code, run tests, even create & review PRs.
They are nothing short of magic:
- They let me build fast: agents will prototype any new feature in ~20 minutes. I truly cannot count the number of features, bugfixes, tests, and tools I’ve (AI’ve?) been able to build because of these agents. For example, AI let me test confusing audio code on macOS and iOS in just a few minutes.
- They let me try crazy things: human teams aim to “fail fast”; agents can fail ultra-fast. I’m happy to test crazy new ideas and throw out what doesn’t work well. It was able to wire & test a huge change to Mumble that added better noise cancelling; I use my beta build of it nearly every day.
- They remove drudgery: I’ve had agents diagnose & fix urgent bugs with nothing more than a description and a “please fix!” while I continued working on other things.
- They let me be kinder: since agents write everything, it is simple to propose sweeping changes to my teammates during code review, or even write my own versions — both things unthinkable in the era of hand-written code.
I do not believe engineering is solved: left to run on their own, agents will build poorly-functioning, over-architected, unreadable, self-congratulatory piles of slop. Every friend I’ve asked agrees that agents still need human taste and experience to produce good work. Some of that is minutiae (like that annoying status dot Claude likes to throw onto sites), but most of it is critical. Agents tend to get lost on their own. My most successful work this year was hand-writing a tool, replacing ~4,000 lines of vibe-code with a few hundred. My system has proven more flexible, easier to test, and more generalizable than what it replaced.
It remains to be seen how long that human edge will last, though.
I also now reckon with the fatigue of using these agents. Managing 6 different conversations with 6 different robots about 6 different features is overstimulating & exhausting in a way that coding never was. When I started using agents, I remember rushing to answer their questions like they were human colleagues waiting for help! While I have tempered that anthropomorphic bias, it’s exhausting to juggle so many problems at once. The allure of sending just one more prompt before lunch… then dinner… oy. There is also, as I wrote in Consider the chairmaker, the decline of craft. My friend Peter laments ceding the joy of programming to machines: for many of us, honing the code, finding the right design, seeing the parts mesh together — that was the meditative purpose we found in our jobs. Now, we rarely write anything. We instead delegate it to agent number 7.
But let me return to the joy of working with agents: they are so fast, so open to feedback, and so intelligent. Working with them can be utterly delightful.
For example, while I was building a harness for voice agents, one programming agent decided (correctly) that my simple test harness was insufficient. So it used my Mac’s built-in text-to-speech to directly test the voice agent it was building. Then, newer agents started doing it, too. Either they had documented the technique, or they were each smart enough to independently discover it. Directly testing the product they were building. Absolutely brilliant.
Agents frequently recommend knobs & settings that I’ll reject for being too complex and unnecessary — and, voilà, I’ll need the knob next week. Silly human!
Anyway, because of agentic coding, agentic pull requests are increasingly the way I review agent code. “Make a draft PR,” I write, “I’ll review it soon!” And review it I do — agents still aren’t reliable enough to trust without validating, so I’ll still review their code & test it manually. However, I don’t do the “line-by-line” code reviews I used to do with humans. I focus instead on architecture, on larger patterns in the code. Are there systemic issues with an approach? Should I add new agent guidance to CLAUDE.md? Can I build better test harnesses, so the machines can test their own code?
Agentic code review is surprisingly helpful here: I try to write rules for the code review robots whenever I notice a recurring issue with generated code, so the agents will identify & fix issues by themselves. One rule I enjoyed creating: a "Claude-y comment detector." You think my writing is verbose? Try Claude’s.
On more typical engineering teams, human code review seems increasingly difficult. A friend of mine complained that his teammates simply ask “their” Claudes to review code written by other Claudes. An ouroboros of Claudes! Agents catch bugs & stylistic issues very well, but they are abysmal at designing architecture. Agentic code review is certainly not a replacement for humans yet.
Last year, I was skeptical of inline editing and code mode, both features of GitHub Copilot. They were not very useful then, and they are even less useful with agents. I have removed them from the table.
|  | Usefulness | Notes | 
|---|---|---|
| Autocomplete | 👍👍 | Still great, obsolete | 
| Agent mode | 👍👍👍 | The most important use of AI today | 
| Agentic PRs | 😒 | Validation loop still slow | 
| Code review | 👍 | Removes some drudgery, but not human-level yet | 
Research & search
Last year, I was excited about research & search: they were the most frequent reason I used ChatGPT. Now, generative AI is the default way I do those things.
The biggest change has been Google’s AI summary. Google’s first or second result is almost always an AI summary, and it’s usually decent. So my traditional search is now AI-first by default. Is it perfect? Absolutely not. In one day, it gave me incorrect URLs for NPR’s RSS feeds and couldn’t find the origin of “AI’ve”.
But none of the top results clearly gave me NPR’s RSS feeds either, and even Claude couldn’t find “AI’ve”. Meanwhile, searching “HP Reverb G2” gave me the specs I was looking for, “ai intelligence is spiky” pointed me to the correct term (“jagged”), “emoji sigh” gave me the right emoji without sending me to a scummy site, and “rel nofollow markdown” reminded me how to link that site without giving them search engine juice.
Product search is still mediocre. I’ll look at the summary when I search “best hysa”, but I don’t trust Gemini to have good advice on where to put my money. Claude certainly helped me explore budget VR options and understand technical details about grease for KitchenAid mixers, but can I trust its coffee table recommendations? Sleeper sofas? Let’s not even mention how uncomfortable it is to see ads in my ChatGPT chats.
Pub facts—stuff I’d ask my wife at a pub — remain awesome with LLMs. Again, Google’s AI summary means “lego cat on a balcony tiktok guy” will help me find @avadonye’s precarious LEGO builds, and “art vtuber who is a lizard on TikTok who gives short tutorials” will help me find Mallow, the art vtuber who is a lizard on TikTok who gives short tutorials.
I often avoid using LLMs for pub facts, in the same way I generally avoided Google for them before, because I like puzzling with my friends. I like Fermi problems.
But I’m more and more excited about using LLMs as teachers to explore well-known concepts. I breezed over this last year, but that is unfair to LLMs. I believe they are the greatest teachers humanity has ever created.
- I had an LLM walk me step-by-step through fine-tuning Mistral to speak like a pirate (yarrr).
- I used Claude to practice responding to an EMS call I heard on the radio.
- I had Claude use a socractic method skill I found via Dan MacKinlay to help me brainstorm new approaches for semantic endpointing (knowing when a user is done speaking) in voice agents.
- I asked Claude to explain typical approaches to a complex legal document.
- I’ve even had Claude quiz me on a long code review, to ensure I understood what the agent had written. The open-source project Mumble actually added a similar quiz to their AGENTS.md a few weeks ago.
I am actually jealous of the endless care & patience that these machines show. I hope we discover how to share this patience with our kids while ensuring our kids still learn. Veritasium’s Derek Muller discusses this in What Everyone Gets Wrong About AI and Learning: AI is incredible at drilling repetitive practice, at giving immediate feedback, of all the things a private tutor can do… if you ask it to.
“The world is full of heavy objects,” he says, “and yet most people are not ripped.”
That is my greatest fear with AI tutoring today. That these machines must be reminded to teach. Per Muller, learning requires Type 2 thinking — enaging the slow, reasoning mode of your brain. This is very difficult. Your body will surreptitiously & continuously nudge you out of this mode. Tutors exist to force you back into it. But ChatGPT exists to do things for you: it is so fine-tuned for that use that it tends to forget “it’s meant to be a tutor”, even when previously asked. What learning may occur when you have both forgotten your desire to learn?
This differs from my biggest concern last year: accuracy. Responses then often had basic factual errors, but that seems less of an issue today. I think there are 2 basic factors:
- I am more AI-literate. I think more of us have a “sense” of what AI can do well, so we avoid the jagged edges. I don’t, for example, trust ChatGPT’s ability to read sparsely-digitized documents from 1867. So I asked hopefully, then basically ignored its findings.
- AI is smarter. Just like in coding, I think we hit an inflection point this year, where models are simply smart enough to answer more things reliably. MAJOR spoilers for Control if you click, but there’s a reason Google’s AI summary of its ending (using Gemini 3, from November 2025) is simple and correct while Bing’s (using ~GPT 4o, from May 2024) is not, conflating the game with its sequel.
This trend extends to literature searches. Last year, I shared my trepidation about using LLMs for complex literature searches. My skepticism remains: these machines have access to everything ever written, so they can support any premise in good faith. Also, it is well-demonstrated that LLMs have default bias, politically or in other fields, like business strategy. I am worried about their ability to subtly impose worldview, either on their own or at the behest of corporations and governments.
Yet LLMs are now my first choice for literature searches. That’s partially because Google searches have that AI summary on top, so I end up reading it, but also because LLMs have been much more effective than traditional search at finding good, nuanced data for me — despite potential bias. You must remember that Google Scholar search kinda sucks: when I started researching Car touchscreens are cheap, not good, for months I could not find any studies beyond one done by an auto magazine—Vi Bilägare. That was despite having worked at a Georgia Tech lab that researched car user interfaces! Especially as they’ve gotten smarter & I’ve developed intuition, LLMs are good finders. Just see Claude’s investigation into human perceptions of latency for me:
Ultimately, though, human experts are still more reliable than agents. That’s how I moved forward with “Car touchscreens”—I asked someone from that GT lab. I’ve also been buying more books, even slightly-obsolete ones like Card, Morgan, & Newell’s The Psychology of Human-Computer Interaction (everyone, including LLMs, cite it) or old editions of Wicken’s Engineering Psychology and Human Performance (via a nuclear consultant I met at a wedding). They ground my research, simply by offering a legible worldview.
And that’s why I’ve been disappointed in AI as collaborator for novel research. AI has harmed some research I’ve been doing.
My team at Salesforce has been working on voice stuff, and I’ve been trying to improve turn detection — understanding when a user is done speaking. That’s a hard problem, and it’s been a great opportunity to read fundamental research on how human conversation works (finally!). AI was great at finding that research and good datasets (though my teammates gave me context the AI never did). And it was great when I asked it to use the Socratic method to help me design my own turn detection model — until, on a whim, I asked: “are there better architectures?” Why yes, yes there were. AI had led me astray.
That’s not the only time AI waylaid me. LLMs could not figure out how to annotate that model’s training data correctly. I spent days going back and forth with them, trying to decide how to separate turns from interruptions. It is embarrassing how simple the problem became after one good discussion with a human teammate. LLMs are not yet good companions when brainstorming complicated things.
It is weird to write this when OpenAI just solved a Millenium Problem, proved a weaker version of another, solved hundreds more, and releases more solutions every day. But those results cost “millions of dollars”: you need to burn tokens, having agents review agents review agents… just to produce something coherent. In my case, I find I enter this “AI fog” where it takes more effort to review the agent’s response than to come up with my own answers.
It is obvious that AI researchers are coming. Just… not today, not with me.
|  | Usefulness | Notes | 
|---|---|---|
| Traditional search | 👍 | It’s now my default, and it’s fine | 
| Product search | ❌ | Still tasteless & untrustworthy | 
| Pub facts | 👍👍 | Still makes me more annoying at parties! | 
| Learning (Explaining well-known concepts) | 🤔👍 | Am I just convincing myself I’m learning? | 
| Literature searches | 👍 | Still can support any claim, but at least it’s not Google Scholar | 
| (new) Novel research | 🤔 | Coming soon, but not yet | 
Summarization & transcription & voice
LLMs (and local models!) remain uninterestingly good at summarization & transcription.
I’ve been using OpenWhispr and Handy to dictate to my computer, especially to talk to my agents. The best models on the planet run on your computer locally, for free. My biggest complaint is that the apps have bugs (hotkeys work inconsistently, etc.). It’s hard to describe a more boring type of success.
My meetings have automatic notes. My friend built a local pipeline to transcribe & search his childhood home videos. Vikram Oberoi built a site (in 2024!) that automatically transcribes NYC city hall meetings. You can do all of these things on your Mac.
However, I have yet to reliably use voice beyond dictation.
There’s a reason my team at Salesforce is researching it: voice is the original modality. It should be a seamless way of talking to these human-like robots. But I have never felt compelled to talk to my robots; it’s never been frictionless or private-feeling or useful enough. Does old-school Siri count?
|  | Usefulness | Notes | 
|---|---|---|
| Summarization | 👍👍 | Boringly good | 
| Transcription | 👍👍 | Great for talking to my coding agents! | 
| (new) Voice | 🤔 | Seems useful, don’t know how | 
Writing
Last year: “ew.” This year: “ew.”
I still do not use AI to write from scratch, nor as an outlining aid, for things I make.
I’ve narrowed this rule a bit from last year. Last year, I argued that LLMs always lacked context and so were poor communicators. With agentic coding, that’s changed. So I’ve had agents document experiments I designed but had no hand in executing, or write READMEs for code they generated end-to-end.
But even that limited exception irks me. I do not like when I stumble upon AI-generated spew, so why should I subject others to it? To that end, I’ve started prompting my agents to identify themselves whenever they write prose, and I often end up rewriting their documents myself (or at least adding an executive summary). That has helped, but I’m not certain it is enough.
In general, I’m surprised how bad AI remains at writing. AI writing is demanding to read: usually plodding, repetitive, and vapid — but then randomly terse and vague, like it doesn’t understand its own words. Agents will so often cite & quote & summarize every paper ever published, then synthesize it all into a mound of nonsense. That is the AI fog I hit: do I misunderstand all these new papers, or did the LLM just serve up some pseudo-profound bullshit? It is bewildering to me that these models can solve generational math problems on one hand, yet utterly fail to describe turn-taking behavior in humans on the other. That is, I guess, their jagged intelligence. They do not reason like we do. They cannot be fine-tuned to speak like we do. So they solve problems we cannot, and share them in reports we struggle to understand.
In any case, it should not be surprising that I do not use AI for writing or outlining in my communication; neither at work nor on this blog. My employer pays me for my ideas, which only I can voice. And I write on this blog for fun. Writing is an art and a skill I enjoy pursuing.
Why would I delegate my voice to a machine that writes tedious dreck?
It’s still great for finding words. Google AI talked me out of writing “hawking off” (which is not an expression) instead of “ceding” later on. But I’m tempering my regard for it as an editor. Despite my positive & worried assessment last year, when I spoke to several friends who asked agents to edit their job applications, their feedback was universally tepid. Agents were sycophantic, reluctant to be critical. And anyone who worked around this (by saying, for example, "my friend wrote this") found that agents offered misplaced, trite advice that lacked nuance. The agents seemed to regress to the mean: helping those with the worst writing and hindering those with the best. The agents were… fine.
As one friend put it:
[AI writing] is as good as it was 3 years ago. Which, when you consider how much everything else has changed since then…
I avoided using AI editors altogether this year, out of fear that they would erase my voice. But I’m increasingly certain they would just blandify it. AI tells remain the same as always (“You’re absolutely right!”), and these machines seem incapable of improvement without substantial guidance. Perhaps it’s survivorship bias, but these very smart machines produce very mediocre writing.
|  | Usefulness | Notes | 
|---|---|---|
| Writing from scratch | ❌ | Still ew | 
| Finding good words | 👍👍 | Still good | 
| Editing | 👍 | Mediocre. I don’t use it. | 
Art & music & video
Finally, art. I still don’t have a good use for image generation.
Last year, I used AI to generate a few odds and ends, but I stopped this year, mostly out of a vague sense of discomfort. I felt like I was ceding opportunities for creativity to the mediocrity machine.
I’ve enjoyed a lot of the low-effort memes I’ve seen; We need more data centers is one of my favorite jokes all year. And AI helped design some useful presentations I attended. But I’m not sure how AI art fits into life on Earth. Last year I thought I saw AI art at a gift shop. Well, now I’ve seen AI Sketchers ads, AI event posters, AI restaurant menus, AI logos for stores and e-sports teams, AI canvases at HomeSense, and AI t-shirts at Walmart. It’s everywhere, and it’s explicitly replacing human art. Gross.
AI music generation is perplexing in the opposite way. Last year, I worried that I would grow equally tired of it. But no! I’m really enjoying some AI music — and so is the rest of the world. The viral San Juan song inspired covers from humans and lip sync videos from “Mila Kunis, Charlie Puth and Jennifer Love Hewitt”. AI has also inspired new genres: I’ve been humming AI is normal technology? (95k views), LGTM (Looks Good to Me) (1.6M), and The Simulation’s Ending (169k) for weeks. As one commenter wrote on OMG! We’ve found other agents (120k):
I think AI art & music are beautiful when they are used as lenses for human creativity, rather than replacements for it. I guessed something similar last year, and I think last year’s music proved me right. As soon as commercialism replaced creativity, I was out. I soured on Eiden XII when they started sharing new “but it hits different” covers weekly, and I got bored of steel coils-style edutainment after hearing the first clone. There’s something cynical and manipulative about a synthetic woman belting “talk me out of dying” when some dude (presumably) makes money every time I play it.
Similarly, I haven’t listened to any of the new Doompop that’s hit my feed. It’s cool when you generate a few songs; less cool when you post every day. It feels like vultures picking ad revenue from the corpse of a good idea.
That is evident in the world of video generation. I largely escaped last year (although my mom got some weird whale-cleaning videos), but now I’m seeing a bunch. I see AI ads all the time — most memorably with horrid horse-people in Sixt ads. I got baited into a video of a fake Edna Mode lookalike & some slop WW2 history videos, and my wife got tricked by AI summaries of Adventure Time marketed as sleep aids. All of them hoping to get views, to get ad revenue, to get — as Corridor Digital puts it—“a little bit skimmed off of that YouTube trough.” It is sobering to open an AI history video in Incognito and gaze at the misleading slop recommended next to it:
It is horrid to see these machines that can mass-produce art being used to mass-produce art. And I know that seems silly, but there’s a world where we use these tools to elevate artists, just like coding agents elevate me.
I am lucky I do not make my living from art. Art remains valuable to me. Even if AI can write a song faster than I can, I still doodle, I still play piano.
Drawin' it yourself is more fun, anyway.
|  | Usefulness | Notes | 
|---|---|---|
| Image generation | ❌ | A net negative so far | 
| Music generation | 👍 | I like it when it’s non-commercial | 
| Video generation | ❌ | Has it ever been used for good? | 
Conclusion
So here we are, 12 months later.
12 months since my first abortive attempts to have agents write code. 10 months since Claude Code first made me say, “wow,” when it built me an insurance comparison tool in one shot. And now machines write 90%+ of my code.
It is easy to forget how new this is. 15 months ago, AI did well at a prestigious high school math competition. 2 months ago, AI solved Navier-Stokes.
Last year, I wrote: “I’m confident we’re just starting to see what AI can achieve.” That remains true. We are just now beginning to see what these mechanized coders and mathematicians can build. My friends have built each other tools to communicate. I was able to finally clean up and share a tool I’d started in 2020. Agents helped me finish up an open-source change I’d wanted to make for years, start making an app, test massive changes to old software, and quickly understand new operating systems.
That is just the start.
It is a brave new world. Where these machines also ship corporate slop and leave mathematicians in shock. But I think of how my uncle uses these tools to build his own software; how my friends make software that helps us stay in touch; how these things have helped me learn so, so much. Tools can be used to help people.
That is how I hope to use AI.

In case you’re wondering, I’m subscribed to:

I cancelled OpenAI about a month ago, which is crazy. OpenAI was my first AI subscription! But most of my personal usage is Claude Code, and I ended up using Claude for random questions instead of ChatGPT. And last year we thought OpenAI was so far ahead!

results.title: Canonical adds FIDO2 hardware key support to Launchpad
results.author: Joey Sneddon
results.content:
Developers who use Launchpad can now use a USB FIDO2 security key to restrict API access, which makes any stolen login details useless without it.
Launchpad is, as I’m sure you know, where Canonical builds Ubuntu’s package, hosts code, PPAs and many other things that end up on a users’ system.
Developer tools, like lp-shell and ubuntu-archive-tools, log in with a saved token, normally kept as a text file or in the desktop keyring on the developer’s machine. Anyone who gets hold of it, malware included, could act as them, with the permissions it carries.
Canonical’s Jürgen Gmach says “for most people that is an acceptable risk”. For core distro dev, engineers and package uploaders? Well, they have more to lose and could become a ‘tempting target’ for bad actors (not the Tommy Wiseau kind).
Which is why Launchpad has added support for hardware-bound API tokens.
These replace the stored token with “a long-lived OAuth refresh grant” that can’t do much without the physical security key attached. Logging in requires touching the key and entering its pin. This issues a short-lived token for everyday requests.
The key protects the stored grant, so malware that ran with the developer logged in could still use any short-lived token for its (brief) lifetime, but it wouldn’t be able to request a new one.
Developers wanting to opt-in will need a supported device (only USB keys are supported; NFC keys and passkeys stored on a device are not) and the python3-fido2 package installed. 
Full setup details are listed in the launchpadlib docs.
results.summary:
Canonical has introduced hardware-bound FIDO2 security key support for Launchpad, allowing developers to secure API access and prevent unauthorized use of stolen login tokens for Ubuntu package management.

### Key Points
- Launchpad now supports USB FIDO2 security keys to protect developer API access and prevent credential theft.
- The new system replaces static stored tokens with long-lived OAuth refresh grants tied to physical hardware.
- Users must touch their security key and enter a PIN to generate short-lived tokens for daily operations.
- The feature currently supports only USB-based keys and requires the installation of the python3-fido2 package.
- This security update specifically targets core distribution engineers and package uploaders who manage sensitive system infrastructure.

### Why it Matters
This update significantly hardens the security of the Ubuntu ecosystem by mitigating the risk of malware hijacking developer credentials. By requiring physical hardware authentication, Canonical reduces the potential for supply chain attacks that could compromise critical software packages.

results.title: Proton VPN 8.0 is coming to iPhone — and it could be the app's biggest upgrade in years
results.author: monicajwrites@gmail.com (Monica J. White) , Monica J. White
results.content:
- Proton VPN has published iOS 8.0.0 on GitHub, but the update is yet to reach the App Store
- Its primary focus is Proton protocols, a new Rust-based VPN engine aimed at stability and censorship resistance.
- An advanced kill switch, an interactive globe map, and better CarPlay support are also on the way.
Proton VPN users on iPhone have a big update to look forward to. The provider has published iOS 8.0.0 on its GitHub releases page, and it could be the most significant change to the app in years.
The biggest addition is Proton protocols, a new VPN architecture that Proton says is designed for improved stability and censorship resistance. It also makes the advanced kill switch possible on iPhone and iPad, a feature that has so far only been available on iOS in beta.
Proton VPN already sits among the best VPN services we've tested, climbing to third place in our latest round of re-testing. Anything that tightens up its iOS app is good news for privacy-minded iPhone owners.
What's new in Proton VPN 8.0 for iOS
The biggest change is one you won't see. Proton protocols, known internally as ProTUN, swaps out the standard wireguard-go code for libpvpnclient, Proton's own WireGuard implementation written in Rust.
Proton says wireguard-go never integrated well with Swift, the language it uses to build its iOS app, which made development and debugging harder.
For users, Proton promises faster updates, fewer platform-specific bugs, and a quicker response when censors change tactics.
The new core also lays the groundwork for post-quantum encryption, which Proton lists as a planned feature. Antonio Cesarano, Product Lead at Proton VPN, says it lets the team experiment with "connection stability, battery usage, and resilience".
A stricter kill switch for your iPhone
A standard kill switch cuts your internet if the VPN connection drops. Proton's advanced kill switch goes further, blocking all internet access unless you're connected to Proton VPN, and it stays active even after you restart your device.
That's a notable step on iOS, where Apple's network restrictions have long made a true kill switch difficult. Proton itself once said a kill switch as it defined it wasn't possible on iOS. Even now, Proton warns that some DNS requests from Apple services can bypass the VPN with the kill switch on.
Version 8.0 also fixes a common frustration. You'll be able to reach LAN devices, like printers, and use Apple CarPlay with either kill switch enabled.
When can you get Proton VPN 8.0?
Proton hasn't announced a release date. However, with the final 8.0.0 build now tagged on GitHub, the App Store rollout could land any time now, though Apple's review process can add a delay.
Monica is a tech journalist with over a decade of experience. She writes about the latest developments in computing, which means anything from computer chips made out of paper to cutting-edge desktop processors.
GPUs are her main area of interest, and nothing thrills her quite like that time every couple of years when new graphics cards hit the market.
She built her first PC nearly 20 years ago, and dozens of builds later, she’s always planning out her next build (or helping her friends with theirs). During her career, Monica has written for many tech-centric outlets, including Digital Trends, SlashGear, WePC, and Tom’s Hardware.

### Key Points
- The update introduces "Proton protocols," a custom WireGuard implementation written in Rust to replace the previous wireguard-go code.

This update represents a significant technical shift for Proton VPN by moving to a proprietary, Rust-based engine that simplifies development and debugging on iOS. By overcoming long-standing platform limitations regarding kill switches and network connectivity, the company is positioning its service as a more robust privacy tool for mobile users.

results.title: Very cold war: Who’s attacking Europe’s supermarket freezers?
results.author: Edna Mohamed
results.content:
Supermarket refrigerators and freezers across Europe have been targeted by a cyberattack that raised the temperature of internet-linked units, destroying and damaging large quantities of food.
On Monday, fridges and freezers at more than 100 shops in several European countries ran hot. Cyberattacks on supermarkets began last month, when hundreds of French supermarkets were left with spoiled food and damage to units which had overheated, costing millions of euros.
So far, it remains unclear why hackers targeted the supermarkets, but attacks have spread across the continent and even to the United States.
Here’s what we know:
Which countries in Europe have been targeted?
On Monday, several supermarkets in Europe were affected, including the following:
- Dutch supermarket operator Delhaize said dozens of its shops in Belgium and Luxembourg were hit by an “IT incident”.
- French retailer Carrefour said about 15 of its 700 Belgian locations were hit by refrigeration problems.
- The Colruyt group, which runs Spar stores in Belgium as franchises, said five of its shops were affected.
- Swedish Coop said cooling systems at seven of its 800 stores were affected, with disruptions ranging from complete shutdowns to partial operation.
- Swedish furniture retailer IKEA, which also operates restaurants at its stores, said one site in Mons, Belgium, had been affected by a cyberattack.
- De Laet & Van Haver, the Belgian butchery chain, said the temperature in its fridges at its store in Hove, south of Antwerp, was raised as high as 18 degrees Celsius, ruining meat worth about 15,000 euros ($16,764).
- The food wholesaler Musgrave said a cyber-incident affected refrigeration systems in 13 of its SuperValu stores in Ireland.
- In October, hundreds of French supermarkets suffered cyberattacks, spoiling tonnes of food, causing fires and melting parts of refrigeration units.
What has happened in the US?
In August, freezers at a market in Fort Huachuca, an Army base in Arizona, went into defrost mode, spoiling all the frozen food they contained, according to a post on Facebook by the base.
The same month, the naval station in Newport, Rhode Island, reported on Facebook that its refrigeration system was affected, leaving only dry goods were available for purchase.
The Pentagon considered the freezer malfunctions on the military bases to be a suspected hack, the Reuters news agency reported late last month, citing four officials close to the matter.
One official said Pentagon investigators were communicating with the French authorities about the issue.
How are cyberattackers targeting fridges and freezers?
Hackers can access the controls of fridges and freezers which use internet software and raise their temperature in order to spoil frozen food.
In some cases, hackers have increased the temperature of appliances to as high as 50C (122F) in European supermarkets, causing them to melt or even catch fire.
Awais Rashid, a professor of cybersecurity at the University of Bristol in the UK, explained that many supermarket refrigeration systems which are remotely managed and, often by third parties, have not been given necessary software updates to prevent hackers.
“In line with established cyber security practices, these systems should be managed via secure networks. However, this is not the case in these incidents and they are accessible on the Internet,” Rashid told Al Jazeera.
“A remote managing party can access a web server on the controller to configure the system including temperature changes and maintenance. There are known vulnerabilities in several controllers (many of which are past their end of life),” he said.
Rashid added that vulnerabilities include “easily guessable” passwords, which would mean anyone could gain access.
Why are hackers doing this?
The motive behind the attacks is unclear, but authorities believe it may be a deliberate attempt to disrupt food supplies.
On Monday, the European Commissioner for Agriculture and Food, Christophe Hansen, said the attacks on fridges were a “deliberate attempt to disrupt” the bloc’s food supply and to undermine consumer confidence.
He added that while “food security is not currently at risk … the food waste and impact on businesses are real”.
Rashid said that while there are few details about who may be behind the attacks or what their motives are, it is likely that these are “the motive here is likely disruption”.
“This has financial impacts on the supermarkets but also societal impacts in terms of security of the food supply chain. Critically, this risks undermining trust in infrastructures on which people rely daily,” he said.
Who is behind the attacks?
On Monday, Belgium’s prosecutor’s office announced that it had opened a criminal investigation into the latest fridge cyberattacks. But so far, no one has taken responsibility.
Theories have emerged linking state actors to cyberattacks generally, with North Korea most recently accused of being behind last week’s $6.3bn Binance cryptocurrency heist, which forced the crypto group to freeze accounts.
European intelligence officials have also warned that Russia is escalating its shadow war on the continent amid the ongoing conflict with Ukraine, with cyberattacks among the methods it uses.
On Tuesday, the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre warned that Britain needs to be prepared for an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered cyberattack on its critical national infrastructure within the next two years.
“By 2028, it is highly likely that Russia, China and other nation states will routinely use AI-cyber to achieve their geopolitical goals, with the UK facing an increase in scale and speed of sophisticated cyberattacks,” the NCSC said in a report.
The report comes shortly after the UK launched its “Be Ready” campaign, calling on citizens to stockpile enough tinned food, bottled water and cash to last three days in the event of a cyberattack or national emergency.
Rashid said that as our infrastructure becomes increasingly digitised, the risk of disruption from cyberattacks, especially “cyber-physical infrastructures such as refrigeration systems”, has risen.
“However, we should also note that a lot of our digital infrastructures operate safely everyday because good security practices enable that. The world works because cyber security works effectively. So it is important that all businesses follow good cyber security practices,” he said.
results.summary:
Cyberattacks targeting internet-connected refrigeration systems across Europe and the United States have caused widespread food spoilage and equipment damage, prompting investigations into potential efforts to disrupt food supplies.

### Key Points
- Hackers are remotely accessing vulnerable refrigeration controllers to raise temperatures, causing food loss and, in some cases, fires in supermarket units.
- Major retailers including Delhaize, Carrefour, Spar, Coop, IKEA, and SuperValu have reported incidents across Belgium, Luxembourg, France, Sweden, and Ireland.
- U.S. military facilities, including bases in Arizona and Rhode Island, reported similar freezer malfunctions that the Pentagon suspects were deliberate cyberattacks.
- Cybersecurity experts attribute the vulnerabilities to outdated software, lack of secure network management, and the use of easily guessable passwords on remote-access controllers.
- Belgian authorities have launched a criminal investigation into the attacks, though no group has claimed responsibility for the disruptions.

### Why it Matters
These attacks highlight the growing vulnerability of critical infrastructure as essential systems like food refrigeration are increasingly digitized without adequate security protocols. The incidents threaten the stability of the food supply chain and demonstrate how cyber-physical attacks can cause significant financial losses and undermine public trust in essential services.
